speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY

That, in the opinion of this House, railway rates westward from the prairie provinces should be reduced to an equality with railway rates eastward from said provinces for similar goods and distances.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY
speechtext:
I share the opinions expressed by the leader of the Opposition in this matter. There are on the order paper three or four resolutions dealing with the coal situation, and I think that this House is entitled to the fullest possible opportunity of discussing this question. There are also two or three other resolutions that are certainly of sufficient national importance to warrant this House going into them. After all, we have been sent here for the purpose of presenting to the House and the country the requirements of the various constituencies which we represent, and I do not think it would be wise at this time wholly to abandon private members' day. Perhaps if one day,

say Wednesday, were abandoned and Monday retained for a little while until the more important resolutions have been dealt with, it would meet the views of hon. members generally. .
Mr. PIERRE F. CASGRAIN (Charlevoix-Montmorency): There is on the order paper a resolution of very great importance, the first one, standing in my name, which proposes the amendment or abrogation of the Bankruptcy Act for the reasons stated in the resolution. On many occasions when the resolution was called I was quite prepared to proceed with it but was requested by certain hon. members who were evidently interested in it, to allow it to stand over until some other day. I. should not like the present motion to carry unless I were given a definite assurance that I should be able to proceed with this resolution. I would suggest that the motion of the Prime Minister be amended by striking out the words "on and," so that the motion would read:
That after Monday the 19th of March instant, to the end of the session, government notices and government orders shall have precedence, etc.
This would give me an opportunity to proceed with my resolution.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY
speechtext:
Under the rules of the House notices of motions by private members have precedence on Mondays and Wednesdays until such time as the government introduces a motion, which is agreed to, to appropriate these two days to itself. It is well known that as far back as confederation-and possibly the system was followed before that time-a fairly reasonable time was allowed to elapse before the government brought in such a motion. When that motion is carried private members' motions can be dealt with only after government business has been disposed of, the result being virtually to debar private members entirely from presenting any resolutions to the House. This year it is my fortune, or misfortune, I do not know which, to have a very important resolution on the order paper. I am anxious to propose that resolution, but if this motion carries I shall be unable to do so. It may be said that I have had ample opportunity to bring it up, but we all know that members have been very busy, and furthermore the resolution that stands in my name is one that calls for considerable preparation. For that reason I have not been prepared to present it sooner. Nor did I think that the government would introduce the present motion as early as they have done. That opinion I based on last year's experience. Last year the session opened on 8th March and it was

Private Members' Day
not until 5th May that the Prime Minister submitted a motion of this kind to take effect on May 15. During that interval private members had an opportunity to proceed with their resolutions twice a week, and I thought that this year an equal length of time would be allowed for the consideration of euch resolutions. Last year we had ten weeks after the beginning of the session in which to discuss our resolutions; on the present occasion the motion to do away with private members' day is introduced six weeks after the opening of parliament. I have been asked more than once during this session by members on both sides of the House when I would proceed with my resolution, and I should be sorry if the fact that I had not moved it sooner-and I could not very well have done so-should preclude any discussion of the important, subject with which that resolution deals. Now, I have no advice to offer the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), but I may be allowed to quote his own words in regard to the subject matter of his motion. On Sth April, 1920, Right Hon. Sir George Foster moved, on behalf of the government then in power, a motion similar to my right hon. friend's. The leader of the Opposition of that day, the present Prime Minister, strongly opposed the motion on the ground that private members had not had sufficient time to present their resolutions. Sir George Foster, in reply to my right hon. friend, made this statement:
Always the experience has been that the leader of the government pays particular heed to the plea that has been made, and in good form and with good grace he allows another week. This squares the matter and nearly everybody is satisfied and amiable and complacent. Now, I am quite willing to do that and to give my hon. friend another week, if he will agree to the motion going through in that amended form.
Hansard then reports the present Prime Minister as follows:
Mr. Mackenzie King: We shall be thankful for small mercies if we cannot get anything better.
Now, I am asking to-day only for a small mercy in the shape of another week at least. I would move therefore that the motion be amended by substituting for the words "the 19th" the words "the 26th," which would give us the whole of next week in which to bring forward private resolutions.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY
speechtext:
The suggestion of the last speaker (Mr, Denis) may be all right so far as he is concerned, but for those of us whose resolutions happen be in the tenth or twelfth place it gives rise to difficulties. In my case I have been quite prepared to go on. I put my resolution on the order paper early in the session but have not had an opportunity to proceed with it.
And I may say that the Acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) assured me that I should be given an opportunity to take the matter up; he said he would see that I got that opportunity. I cannot see, however, how he can carry out that undertaking if private members' day is abandoned. I therefore strongly advocate the retention of private members' day at least once a week for a reasonable period in order that hon. members may have a chance to clear up the resolutions that were placed on the order paper in the early stages of the session.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree largely with the last words which dropped from the lips of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauv-reau), with the qualification that I do not think they have any application to my own motion. maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, not 10 per cent of the time taken up with private members' motions has been devoted to motions presented by hon. members in this quarter of the House; most of the time has been devoted to resolutions introduced by the Progressives on purely academic questions. I have a resolution on the order paper, No. 11, in which ninety per cent of. the people of Canada are vitally interested. I have had many representations from municipalities and other public bodies requesting me to bring this matter to the attention of the House, but so far I have had no opportunity to do so. The resolution was called one day, but I could not proceed because the Prime Minister had arranged to give another motion precedence. I should like an early prorogation, but I do urge on the Prime Minister that he set apart an afternoon or an evening for the discussion of this very important question. I think it is only fair to the government that the country should know what it has been doing, and that an opportunity should be given for hon. members to present constructive suggestions on how to avoid a repetition of the disastrous conditions which have prevailed this winter through the lack of an adequate supply of fuel-conditions which will be still more disastrous next winter unless we take proper measures to ensure an adequate supply of coal.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope that the Prime Minister wall accede to the request made by a number of members to extend the time for another week for the discussion of private members' resolutions. If the Prime Minister does not consent, I hope that the amendment offered will be voted on, for I shall certainly vote for an extension of another week.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may be allowed, I should like to make a suggestion. After an extensive experience in the House I have come to the conclusion that the government would be well advised, if they would avoid this annual discussion, to amend the rules to the effect that when a motion has been called for a third time, and not proceeded with, it be dropped from the order paper. The circumstances quoted by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) apply in every case-the government of the day finds itself generally obliged to give one week longer for the discussion of private members' resolutions at the request of various members who have resolutions standing in their name on the order paper. Of the resolutions now on the order paper notices of nine were given in January, and they have all been called since then; twelve in February, and seven this month. These resolutions would all have been proceeded with if their sponsors had been ready. The only exceptions are one or two in regard to which an arrangement was made with the government to take them up on a special date. Therefore I think the only course open to the government to avoid this recurring trouble is to amend the rules in the manner I have suggested.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, although I have a resolution on the order paper, I think the time of this House has already been taken up sufficiently by hon. members speaking longer than they had any right to do. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I need hardly say that the government has no motive in presenting this motion other than to expedite the business of parliament. There is no desire to deprive hon. members of any of their privileges. But I do submit, there is very much force in what has been said about

Private Members' Day
the number of times that many of these resolutions have been called, and it is hardly fair to the House as a whole that the business generally of parliament should be delayed in order that hon. members who have not taken advantage of their turn when it came should have this further extension of time. However, the government, I need hardly say, has no desire to press this motion unless it is going to carry, and from the discussion which has taken place I gather that possibly it is the consensus of opinion that some further extension of time should be granted-one day possibly, certainly not more than two days. If it would meet with the general approval of the House I would be prepared to amend the motion by changing the 19th to the 26th, thus allowing an additional week.

Mr. Speaker, I am not at all sure that would meet the situation. I quite agree with my right hon. friend that a lot of these motions have been called many times, but I do not think the time of the House has been wasted in consequence; if I remember rightly, we went on with estimates and made considerable progress. Usually, private members' days are taken because the government has some real object in view; that is, there is government business that the House is seized of waiting to be done, and suffering by delay. I see no [DOT] such business on the order paper at the present time. The .government list is not at all long, and we have not any bills down that I know of. The Bank Act amendment bill has not been distributed yet; Speaking generally we have really had no government business outside of estimates. We usually hear about the budget speech before this motion is made; this year we have not heard a word as to the approximate date when the budget will be brought down. Yet the privileges of hon. members are to be taken from them. We do not want to delay progress, but I would point out that motion No. 11, in the name of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church), deals with the question of the coal supply. That is not an academic question; it is a matter of immediate importance, and an opportunity for its discussion should be afforded. If we are to have only two more private members' days, it means that the debate on the resolution respecting the Senate will take up the whole of one day, one other motion will take up the next day, and the motion with respect to the coal supply will not be reached. We know how futile these resolutions respecting
the Senate are. If the government can assure us that the motion on coal will be dealt with, that meets the case so far as I am concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY
speechtext: I think the subject to which my hon. friend has just referred was considered at some length in the course of another debate in the House, and doubtless in other connections it may come up again. It is reasonable to expect that we can rely on the good judgment of those who have resolutions on the order paper not to take up too much of the time of the House in dealing with them. If hon. members will be seized of what appears to be the general wish they will be short in their speeches and not devote more time than is necessary to their resolutions. Certainly any resolutions in respect to which there has been an understanding should be taken up; where the suggestion has been made that they be held for consideration later, it would be desirable to arrange that they be dealt with. Apart from that, however, it seems to me that if an additional week is given, involving an additional two days for members' resolutions, that would meet the situation. I would like to move, therefore, with the permission of the House, to substitute "26th" for "19th" and to present the motion in that form.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAY
speechtext:
I have no objection to the resolution being amended, but I am opposed to it as amended, because there will not be time for reasonable discussion of important resolutions. This, I think, is the earliest that this motion has ever been pressed -I speak only from recollection; I have not checked the dates-and it is done in a session in which the government business has been expedited the most. That is to say, there has been on the part of hon. members less delay of government business than I have ever seen in this parliament. Not only has there been nothing in the way of obstruction, but every facility has been given for reasonable progress, and the progress has been rapid, in a session when there is less government business than there has been, perhaps, in any session for years. There are only the estimates, and there is a bill regarding combines; what else is there? There are two others that are being considered by committees, but that is all we have this session. It is true that if a motion is called and passed by, and the House has then to adjourn, time is lost, but if the House simply gets to another resolution that is disposed of, or if it gets to government business, time is not lost; and that has been the practice this session.
Easter Adjournment

I do not know that I can preface my remarks on the question of immigration now before the House, in a better way than by reading to the Committee an editorial from the Montreal Star of Tuesday, February, 13, 1923. It is very short, and I trust that the members of the Committee will bear with me while I put it on Hansard;
51st Month
It is now fifty months since the armistice. The cessation of war should have been Canada's golden opportunity to increase her population.
Australia and New Zealand seized the opportunity and are benefiting enormously, adding huge capital accretion to the national assets. Canada with folded arms has stood still. The old coalition government attempted nothing, did nothing and did'nt want to do anything. The Liberal government has shut its eyes to the situation, permitted the waste of time of enormous value, then attempts to propitiate the public by promises that mean nothing but delay and suggest nothing but cowardice in dealing wtih the greatest problem that ever confronted the Canadian people.
If the Liberals are to be as inert as the Conservatives or Coalitionists, our country will never take its natural place amongst progressive nations. This Dominion needs a saviour. Its best interests have been neglected.
There has one come now.

Does the hon. gentleman refer to me? I should not be the first of my race that acted as such.
I was glad to note from the remarks of the Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Stewart) that he did not dignify the proposition which he brought down on Wednesday last by the name of a policy. We have no policy before this country in the matter of immigration. During the tenure of office of the Union government, and later of the National Liberal and Conservative government-as I think they called themselves- nothing was done at all, absolutely nothing; and it gave me a splendid opportunity to make attacks from time to time upon the ineptitude of that government, and I took

occasion to predict that when our party came into power the fog and miasma, if I may call it such, of Unionism would yield to the sunshine of Liberalism.
Before the hon. gentleman gets to that much more appropriate subject, will he tell the House the actual number of immigrants secured during the time he is complaining of?

I do not think the number of people who came into the country during that period is a fair test of the immigration which was received, because the war held up for a number of years a large number of people who were in Europe, from coming to this country. I do not think it is quite fair that the Union government should claim that all these people who came back including even the soldiers, should be looked upon as regular immigrants.

There is none of that kind claimed at all, and the records do not include them. The records only include immigrants who are immigrants, that is, those who have come for the first time to settle in this country. The hon. gentleman knows that. There is none in the House knows it so well.

If they came in, they came in notwithstanding the protest of the government. I had myself a great deal to do in bringing some of them in. In any event we expected nothing from that government, and we got what we expected. But at the present moment when we have here, in "the seats of the mighty," on the treasury benches a galaxy of all the talents of the Liberal party, I must express my surprise and my astonishment that we are simply following in the way of the Philistines,-nothing is being done at all. We have a commercial proposition put before us: We are going to go into partnership with a company known as the Canada Colonization Association
No, no.

-a company which has no president so far as I know, and has no general manager. It is a company which shows its astuteness in many ways worth while. As I understand it they have received large sums of money through the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. I believe a call was made on members of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association to give their support, in a monetary sense, to this organization. Each member of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association was invited to contribute according to the number of men in his employ to this patriotic

movement. In that respect, as I say, they show a considerable degree of commercial ability. To extract large sums of money from the members of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association is in itself no mean feat.

Can the
hon. member inform the House exactly how much was extracted from this association?

Well, *it is rather difficult
to find out how much money the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and its members contributed to the public weal; I am not in a position to say. 1 do know, however, that a call has been made throughout the country for support for this patriotic scheme and-[DOT]

The hon. gentleman said
that an assessment has been levied. What proof has he of that?

I have the statement from a member of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association who was asked to contribute $15,000 to this scheme, that is, in proportion to the number of people whom he employed; and he said he promptly ushered to the door the gentleman who applied. I do not know whether the hon. member himself has contributed any such sum as that. He would probably know and I am sure we would be glad to learn from him what the amount was.
I can tell the hon. gentleman, not one cent. The hon. gentleman said that a levy was made. I object to that statement. I do not think it is true, and I do not think it can be substantiated.

I did not mean to convey
the impression that a levy was made, it was just a friendly application to members who felt that this was a worthy object. Well, after this work was concluded we find that the president of this colonization association, Sir John Willison, retired precipitately from the presidency-why, I do not know. The minister in discussing this matter the other day did not give any information to the House as to why this organization, which will have hundreds of thousands of dollars of the money of the people of Canada, has no president. That is something, I think, which the country itself would like to be enlightened about. Without a president they nevertheless went on- probably they found that they could get along as well without a president; it may be they felt that it would be better for their purposes if they jettisoned Sir John Willison. They eame before the Department of Immigration and secured $100,000, with the understanding that they would obtain 200 families

Supply-Immigration
to settle on the land. Well, 200 families do not seem to be a very large number when we consider that during last year as many as 10,000 people have left the farms and towns of Canada in one month to go to the United States. In any event we are to be out our $100,000. I am not complaining particularly about that phase of it: "Any port in a storm;" "A drowning man will grasp at a straw.". The minister had no policy at all to bring before the government, he felt that anything was better than nothing; and when the
4 p.m. Canadian Colonization Association showed up he looked upon them as friends of his because, to a certain extent, they helped him out of the situation in which he found himself just previous to the meeting of parliament.
I want to say this, Mr. Chairman, before going very much further: I feel like the father who was about to chastise his child- it pains me more than it does the child. It is not a very pleasant matter for me, a Liberal of many years standing, to get up and snipe my party and the minister from my seat in the House. But this is something that transcends party, this is a national problem. I feel very strongly upon this question of immigration. I have discussed immigration ever since I came into the House. I have delivered what I might claim to be my annual address on this subject to the House ever since 1918. So far my words have fallen on deaf ears; I am a voice in the wilderness. But I trust that in time the government will see that this is a matter which vitally affects every person in this Dominion, and that unless we awake to the seriousness of the situation we may find ourselves before long in the shades of opposition-I was going to say, which we will fill so acceptably, but which we did fill for an entire decade. We will find that our kingdom will have been taken from us, and that some persons considered more worthy to reign in our stead will be occupying the government benches.
Look over this way please.

I want to tell my hon. friend the leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) that if he is prepared to accept my policy on the immigration question, I will go over to his side of the House and support him on that question. In fact, in order to show how seriously I look upon this matter, I would go so far as to join the Labour group in the other part of the chamber if I found they would do something for immigration.
This w'hole question of immigration has become acute, Mr. Chairman, owing to the
conditions which have been brought about in the United States through the closing of their doors to immigration of all kinds. Ever since the American government put the three-per-cent quota into effect we have been suf-ferring from it, and I will tell you why: The United States, for over a hundred years, have had their doors open to immigration. They have received vast numbers of immigrants of all kinds, of all classes, from Europe, and they have incorporated them into their nation and made men out of them. Suddenly the door is closed. People who have been accustomed to receiving hundreds of thousands of workmen find that they cannot get them any longer, and where do they turn? They turn to the north, and in that way our people are being drawn off the farms and from the cities in order to supply the demand for people in the United States. That is why 10,000 people a month are leaving our country and going to the United States where they are attracted by very large wages. I am told that in some of the border cities of the United States carpenters receive from $12 to $20 a day as wages. How is it possible for us to keep our people in this country when they are attracted by such enormous wages on the other side of the line? We in our unwisdom felt that what is good enough for the United States is good enough for us, and we put up the bars in almost the same sense as the people of the United States. We carefully scrutinize, we microscopically examine every workman who wishes to come into this country to take the place of those who go to the United States. That is why our people are being attracted from the farms and from the cities in Canada to the larger fields in the countiy to the south. Now, if the minister would realize what is going on he probably would not, with a mere wave of the hand, tell us that in this country there is no room for artisans, no room for city labour, but that what we have to do is to concentrate our energies on settling people on the land.
I point this out to the minister. As soon as wre have those people located on farms, they find that things, particularly in the West and, in fact, throughout Canada, in the farming line, are not what they were led to believe, and they flock into the cities in order to obtain the larger wages which are given to all classes of labour in the cities.

Higher
wages and shorter hours.

Yes, the glare of the gaslight, the movies, and the general social life in the cities. That is what attracts people
Supply-Immigration

from the farms. I venture to predict that if you colonize the West within the next three or four years with half a million farmers, it will be a question of only a very short time when a large body of those people will find their way into the cities, on the principle that if you place two bales of hay in front of a donkey, the animal will make for the larger bale of hay. Why do people go into farming? Because they feel they can make a living. They leave the farms because they feel they can do better in the cities. A farmer who makes $1,500 or $2,000 a year on the farm, working himself, his wife and his children from five o'clock in the morning until sundown or even late at night, is entitled to something more than $1,500 or $2,000. But if that farmer, his wife and his entire family were to locate in a city, they could make twice that amount of money, with shorter hours, better conditions and a better social life.
My suggestion to the minister is that at the time when he is seeing to it that people are placed on the farms, he should also see to it that vacant positions in the cities are filled by people who are accustomed to live in the city. In that way, the farmers will not be attracted to the cities, because the positions there will be taken up. But if you have a vacancy in one place and place an opportunity for leaving in another, it is only natural that the vacancies will be filled particularly if it is found more profitable to fill them. If you make farming pleasant and profitable, and if you surround it with all the advantages which life in this country can give, you will attract people to those farms and those waste places. At the same time, if you see to it that positions in the cities are filled by city dwellers, then you have solved the problem. But nothing of the kind is being done, and the reason of it is that, as our dear old friend Sir Sam Hughes used to say in this House: "There is an unseen and hidden hand somewhere that is arresting the progress of the government." He liked to dwell on the unseen hand.
Would the hon. member be so kind as to deprive the farmer of an opportunity of bettering his condition by going into the city, by bringing in a considerable number of men to fill up the cities?

The question is one of the survival of the fittest. I am looking after the interest of the country as a whole, not after that of any particular farmer. I believe the farmer in the end is very much happier on the farm than when he comes into the city. He does not see the thing in that way; but after a while, after it is too late, he comes to realize that he should never have left the farm.
fMr. Jacobs.]
How could the farmer be so happy when the hon. member has mentioned all the social conditions that exist in - the cities and the very different conditions on the farm?
The farmer must work out his own salvation in that regard.
The hon. member, then, is, trying to work out the salvation of the country.

It must be made profitable for the farmer to live on his farm. His freight rates must be reduced to such a figure that he can actually live on the farm. I am not altogether a free trader yet; I have not been converted to that school of thought; but we must reduce, to a certain extent, the tariff on his agricultural implements, his implements of production, and do other things of that kind.
To what extent-two and a half per cent?

I shall be glad if my hon. friend will come to my room to-morrow, when we can discuss the whole matter fully, and I am sure we shall arrive at a conclusion which will be satisfactory to us botlj. We have been told that we are going to have farm labourers brought to this country. That is one of the planks in the platform, if I may so call it, of the department. Would the Acting Minister of Immigration tell me what he is going to do with farm labourers if there are no farms? The farmers are scarcely able to maintain themselves, on their farms, working with their own families. How then are they going to pay farm labourers if farming is not profitable ? Farming is a seasonal occupation. The farm labourer is used for the seeding and for the harvest, and at the end of that time there is, in a general way, not very much work for him to do. He accordingly finds his way into the city. He is not accustomed at first to doing anything else and he forms a queue for the soup kitchen and the bread line, when unemployment is rife, because it is this class of people not accustomed to city life and who do not know how to cast about when times of stress come on, who are filling up our cities and who create the unemployment question. They are the very first people who come into the cities to swell the tide of unemployment.
Then we are going to bring in female domestic servants. I ask the Minister of Immigration how long he thinks a female domestic is going to be employed in service at $20. $25 or $30 a' month, when that young woman can go into a factory and get twice

Supply-Immigration
that salary with reasonable hours of living, eight hours a day, and instead of receiving $5 or $6 a week, she perhaps receives $30, $35, or $40 a week. How long can you keep such women in domestic service? Why not say to them: "Come into the country; look about for yourselves. If you want domestic service, enter domestic service. If you want to enter factories, enter factories." But to have watertight compartments , such as are sought to be built by the minister, in which it is declared that this person must go into this service and that person into that, is a mistake; it is against the law of nature and all economic law and it will never succeed. The result will be that we shall always be without domestic servants and without farm labourers, and these people will be filling the factories where they can secure large wages.
I have spoken about the hidden and unseen hand. I should like to read to the committee something which will show the African in the woodpile. This is a despatch from Ottawa, dated January 28, and headed:
Tom Moore fears cheap labour here. Immigration policy would open the door to it, he says.
The despatch reads:
Ottawa, January 28.-Speaking here Saturday night, Tom Moore, president of the Dominion Trades Congress, expressed his views on the Canadian immigration policy. An analysis of a statement made by Sir Edmund Walker showed that the immigration policy was really the opening of the door to admit cheap labor, Mr. Moore contended.
While it has been said that Canada wanted settlers for the land, the lid was being lifted by prominent financial men who wanted more settlers to reduce the labor costs, and Mr. Moore urged that the admission of all classes of immigrants would not be beneficial to Canada, for if cheap labor was allowed in to compete with the established citizens, living conditions could not be ameliorated. The speaker reviewed the achievements of organized labor in Canada, stating that great difficulties had been surmounted and the lot of the workingman greatly improved.
I should like to say a word or two in regard to that. In passing, I might say that this gentleman is now a director of the Canadian National Railways.	'v
Who appointed the gentleman?

I do not think that requires any answer. When this gentleman spoke I rather fancy he spoke as president of the Trades and Labour Council and not as a director of the Canadian National Railways. I do not know whether he has yet converted Sir Henry Thornton to his views, but there is room for conversion, because the last time I heard Sir Henry Thornton speak he was in favour of a strong and vigorous immigration policj^ not restricted to the farms. I must
express regret that a director of the National Railways should declare himself on matters of this kind. It is not fair to the country; it is, not fair to those interests that are advocating a proper immigration into Canada; and by reason of the fact that he is a director of the Canadian National Railways, what he says carries more weight probably than it otherwise would. This man is a paid official of the Trades and Labour Council. He is a sort of glorified walking delegate. He is paid for this purpose, and it is his duty to keep wages as high as possible if he thinks that will enure to the benefit of labour generally. But I must express the fear that Mr. Moore, occupying the high position that he does, is not very much of an economist. He ought to know' that where wages are inflated as they are now everything is proportionately dear. For instance, the labourer who pays $40 to $45 a month for his dwelling, which is really worth only $15 or $20, pays the higher rate because he cannot obtain dwellings at any lower figure, the reason being that we do not permit people to come into this country to build houses. There is a scarcity of builders in Canada. You cannot get people to build because they are all going to the United States to get the high wages to which I have referred. So that, although the labourer gets $45 or $50 a week for his work, it is, I venture to say, materially less in reality than the $20 he got before the war. Let us look at the situation. The farmer has already undergone the deflation process. He is obliged to sell his products at 60 to 70 cents in the dollar, but is obliged to pay for the commodities he has to buy, such as manufactured products, not 100 cents, but 150 cents, in the dollar. Why? Because we are obliged to pay labourers more than they are worth. And if you do not cut down the prices of commodities by reducing wages, how is it possible for the farmer ever to get on? It cannot be done. Deflation must take place equally and equably all along the line. But where there is this lop-sided deflation you are bound to suffer as you are suffering now in the West. So that Mr. Moore does not understand the economic situation at all; he is killing the goose that lays the golden eggs. We cannot very much longer stand the conditions that are now prevailing. You pay for your clothing, your boots and shoes, and everything that you need more than twice what you paid for them before the war, but you are getting for your products just the same' as you got at that time. And that is going to go on so long as we do not get the cost of labour reduced to the same proportion as the prices of farm commodities.
Supply-Immigra tion
Does the hon. member say that we Should have lower wages in this country?	.

I am saying that we ought to have the same ratio of wages for labourers as the farmer gets for his products. The present condition is ridiculous. What is the use of getting $50 a week wages when you have to pay i't all out for your upkeep?

Does the hon. gentleman not think that it would be better for us all round if, instead of reducing the wages of labour to what the farmer receives for his work, we raised the farmer's returns in keeping with what labour receives?

The hon. gentleman ought to know that the prices of farmers' commodities are fixed in the world's market. Liverpool fixes the prices for farm produce; they are not fixed in Canada. You are confronted with the Argentine, with Russia-at least you will be faced with Russia shortly if not now-with Italy and every other producing country in the world; and it is idle for us to say that we can fix prices here. We tried to fix prices through a Board of Commerce and we know what happened. It cannot be done; Nature must take its course; and I leave this thought with hon. gentlemen of the committee, trusting that they will see that there is something in the argument I have tried to make.
I think that if you reduced the wages of the working man you would decrease his buying power and the farmer would consequently get less for what he sells.

How could a reduction in the wages of the labourer decrease his buying power if there were a deflation all round? If he gets, say, $30 a week for his labour and has to pay $10 or $12 for a pair of boots for each of his children, himself and his wife, $40 or $50 for his suit of clothes, and $10 a month for rent, supposing he got half that amount in wages, how could his buying power be reduced if all these other expenses were proportionately lowered?-if he paid $20 a month for his house, $20 for a suit of clothes, $5 for boots, and so forth. After all, what is money? It is simply purchasing power; considered in any other light it is nothing. And if the labourer could purchase with $25 exactly what he can get under present conditions for $50, wherein is his purchasing power reduced?
Does the hon. gentleman advocate a simultaneous reduction all round, or is the workingman's wages to be reduced first?

I am now advocating the bringing in of people and letting them fend for themselves. If we had 100,000 persons brought into this country at the present time, does the committee not see how the wheels of commerce would be accelerated? We should have to have dwellings for these people, they would have to be set up in business, and everybody would be doing something until they got to work and produced for themselves. We have more than enough in this country for every one who wants to come and work. But through the narrow-sighted policy of our governments we have interfered with the natural laws governing immigration and we find ourselves therefore in the present deplorable conditi.on. Someone the other evening referred to the alleged lowering of the standard of living. May I refer the member who introduced that question to an address of Sir Clifford Sifton delivered in Montreal on February 26 in which he speaks of the standard of living. He is reported as follows:
"Criticism is made," said Sir Clifford, "that these people have not as high a standard of living as our own people have. A lot of nonsense is talked on that score. They will have the standard of living of pioneers, and what they can get out of the soil. You cannot get the higher standard of living out of that soil I speak of. and you must get the man who will be satisfied with what he can get from it if you are going to settle it.
"That standard of living would probably be as good as that of the men who were the pioneers of Ontario and Quebec. My own ancestors were Ontario pioneers, and they did not worry about standards of living, but cleared the land, and when they had time they built schools and churches and otherwise laid the foundations for the present conditions. They suffered hardships, but they made a prosperous Christian community, and turned out men whose names have become household words in the history of Canada.
Now, with regard to the complaint that we have unemployment so extensively at the present time that it would be dangerous to bring more people in, I would say that this is one of the stock arguments of our friends who wish to repress immigration into our cities. In this connection I may cite a report of a debate in the Ontario legislature on February 13th. I quote the heading as well as the report itself:
Plenty of work on Ontario farms: $35 to $40 a month and board; farmer can't give more. Must get men.
"There is plenty of employment in Ontario but unfortunately there are a considerable number of men vho are not in a position to take advantage of the ipportunities of employment offered," said Premier Drury yesterday in the House.

Supply-Immigration
It was an interesting discussion bringing out a sharp difference of opinion as to whether there was an unemployment problem or not. Several labor members claimed that there was a pressing problem of men out of work and quoted a re'cent return that ten thousand people were unemployed.
Minister of Agriculture Doherty, on the other hand, while admitting there were people without jobs, explained that about thirty applications a day were being received by his department from farmers seeking farm help and it was imposible to supply this demand.
The debate started when K. K. Homuth (South Waterloo) read from the Liverpool Echo an interview given by S. Harris, of the Canadian Army and Navy League, that there was no unemployment in Canada at present except those who would not work. He contended that there was unemployment and people should not be encouraged to come to Canada at the present time. "There are a great number of farmers," said Sam Clarke (West Northumberland) "who would be tickled to death"-
The words are his, not mine.
-to get men who could do the work at $40 to $50 a month and their board. But they cannot get them. There will be a 20 per cent shortage of labour on the Ontario farms by April 15. People can get any amount of work out in the country and if the people would only realize that $2 a day in the country is as good as $4 a day in the city, and keep away from the cities, there would be no unemployment.
G. G. Halcrow (Hamilton East) read a reply from the Minister of Labour that the average wage paid by the farmers was $8.36 a week, with board, and continued.
"As far as I am concerned, I would not be willing to leave a wife and family in the city facing rents and high cost of living and go out to work in the country at $8.36 a week. I would rather stay in the city and all starve together."
"Move them all out," Mr. Clarke interjected.
''There is work in this province for every man who is able to do the work that is offered him," said Mr. Doherty. "If the farmers are to get the labour they need we must bring in people who are prepared to work on the farm. The farmers are paying $35 to $40 a month and board, which is exceedingly fair, in fact, it is only because they are sorely in need of help that they are offering this amount, in view of the low prices they are receiving for their products."
I think that is an effective answer to those who say we have unemployment in the cities. We have people idle in the cities, it is true, but if men engaged in seasonal occupations have an opportunity to go out on the farms and earn money I see no reason why they should not seize the opportunity; and if they ignore it, I do not see why we should concern ourselves further with them, indeed, we ought to wash our hands of them altogether. Undoubtedly it is our duty to see that work is provided for them, but not a paticular kind of work or work in a particular location.
Another citation with regard to unemployment. This is an article from the Gazette of February 28th, incorporating a report from the Dominion Statistician. It says:
According to reports received, compiled and tabulated by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics employment at the beginning of February showed considerable revival from the contractions recorded at the commencement
of January, when losses incidental to the holiday and mid-winter inventory period, supplementing seasonal declines, had reduced activity to a marked degree. The reaction was somewhat more pronounced than that registered at the beginning of February of last year, and considerably more so than at the same period in 1921. Statements for the month under review were compiled from 6,253 employers of labour whose pay-rolls aggregated 733.063 persons as compared with 707,859 at ihe commencement of January. This increase of over 25,000 workers caused the index number to gain slightly over three points, standing at 89.5 as compared with 86.3 on January 1, and with 78.9 on February 1, 1922. Practically all the recovery was recorded in the manufacturing industries, (notably in iron and steel), but logging and coal mining also afforded more employment. Activity in transportation and construction continued to decline, although the shrinkage was on a rather smaller scale than in the preceding months.
This would go to show that we really have no unemployment situation at the present moment.	.
My hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) referred the other day to the fact that there are 6,000 unemployed people in the city of Winnipeg. We all know that during periods of depression the unemployed from the country districts flock into the cities. Winnipeg has a population of 250,000, and the district round about must comprise, I should judge, nearly 1,000,000 people, when we take in the Eed river and the Assiniboine and Saskatchewan river valleys. Out of all those people in that district merely 6,000 were found to be unemployed in the city of Winnipeg-a negligible number.
Now, we must investigate and find out why those people are unemployed. As is well known, we have a large number of returned soldiers, men broken by their military service overseas. It is impossible to get them to remain in any vocation. They wander about, their former life having unfitted them for steady employment. Then we have the human flotsam and jetsam found in all large cities: these people never work. Of course, they have to be provided for in a certain way, but if we are to be deterred from encouraging immigration by there being a few hundred unemployed people in this or that part of the country, why, we shall never have any practical immigration policy.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that I have already taken up too much of the time of the committee in discussing this subject, but it is one on which I feel very strongly, as my friend, the Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Stewart) knows. He,has in various orders in council a number of rules prohibiting people from entering this country. All kinds of what I would call if I were permitted-I have been permitted and I have called them before-fool regulations, nonsensical rules. Those rules do not accomplish the purpose

Supply-Immigration
intended, but they keep out very many people who would be valuable acquisitions to this country- For instance, one order in council declared that no person unless possessed of $250 could enter this country. I understand that this order has been abrogated. But in place of this monetary qualification, another regulation quite as good, even better, has been put in force. After all, $250 is not a very large sum of money for a person to have in his possession. I have known of cases where $250 did a great deal of good, and in fact the same, sum was instrumental in enabling many immigrants to pass the immigration officers. Now it is not necessary to be possessed of $250 in order to enter this country. In place of that regulation we have something much more effective as a restriction. No man of the artisan class who is not a British citizen can come to Canada unless his passport has been vised by the Canadian agent before the immigrant goes aboard his ship. That, I admit, is a very effective restriction. If the artisan is a British citizen he can enter, although even a British citizen used to be debarred unless he possessed $250. If he is an American citizen he does not require the $250 either. The United States take in as many Canadians as are prepared to go there; the Dillingham Act. I understand, does not apply to citizens of our country. But when a Canadian who has left Canada and gone to the United States attempts to come back to his own country he is prevented from doing so on the ground that he has lost, as the order in council says, his domicile-and that is what the minister calls a proper rule. Last year we barred 10,000 Americans from entering Canada at the border-why, I do not know; probably for the reason that from the point of view of their occupations or callings there were no openings for them in Canada at the time. Now, there are hundreds and thousands of people who could come into this country and earn a living as well as any of us can, and who would be an asset to Canada. I do not say they would engage in work in factories, or that they are of the artisan class, but they are small traders, small merchants and so on, who may have been crowded out by the conditions in the United States and elsewhere and who want to get a foothold here. People of this class have always made a success in Canada, but they are not permitted to come in. And, who, do you think, decides whether or not there is a vacancy for a member of the artisan class who seeks entry into Canada? The Department of Labour, so worthily presided over by my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). When an applica-

tion is made for an artisan to come into the country a report is asked for from the Minister of Labour. He probably turns the thing over to the Trades and Labour Council, of which Mr. Tom Moore is the president, and in due course we are notified that there is no vacancy for that particular person and that it is not in the public interest that he be permitted to come in. Is it any wonder that I protest against rules of this kind? We have a lopsided system that will never work. We have a watertight scheme that is bound to fail, because it is not natural. I hope the minister will realize that before it is too late.
Before the hon. gentleman leaves the question of passports to immigrants from central Europe, may I ask what is the effect of the regulation to which he refers?
The effect of it is this: the Canadian official has his instructions and he will not vise their passports, and the result is that the intending immigrants cannot get on board the vessel.
What information is before the Canadian official to show that that sort of man is not wanted in this country- provided he does not know otherwise?
He has the information supplied to him from time to time by the Department of Immigration.

speechtext: May I be permitted to make a correction? I am prepared to sit here and take all this warm medicine, and when hon. members get through I shall have a few things to say. But there is one statement made by my hon. friend that I cannot allow to pass. The instruction given to the agents on the Continent is that there is a place in Canada for physically and mentally fit people from the countries from which we have been accepting immigration. In fact we have been accepting immigrants from former enemy alien countries in cases where their friends were prepared to guarantee that they would be respectable and decent citizens in Canada. But there is no bar on the physically and mentally fit individual who wishes to come to Canada to farm or to seek employment as a farm labourer.

I admit there are no restrictions at all; if a person wants to go on a farm or become a farm labourer, he gets in without any trouble and in due course he finds his way to the city. What I want to have is a direct route.

What I mean is this: when they get on the farm they cannot make the farm pay; then they drift into the city. That has been the burden of my complaint during the whole of this afternoon. We have tens of thousands of persons of British and Canadian stock who started on farms in Canada and who are now in the cities. It is not reasonable, therefore, to conclude that those who come here to go on the land, subjecting themselves to the rigors of the West, having no knowledge of the conditions or of farming in a large way such as is carried on in that part of the country-at best they have been engaged only in intensive farming or market gardening

it is not reasonable, I say, to conclude that these people will remain on the farms but will find their way to the cities. I venture to say that ninety per cent of the members of this House to-day were born on a farm or at one time lived on a farm, but ultimately wandered away to improve their position in life. The hon. Minister of Immigration himself, started out as a farmer; now he is a statesman. Why did he not stay on the farm? Because l}e found it more pleasant and more profitable to become a statesman; and here he is. I venture to say that fifty per cent of the people who are now on farms to-day in the Canadian West would, if they had the opportunity, flock into the cities and help to swell the urban population. I know something of what farming is in the West. It may be a surprise to many hon. members to know that I myself was born on a farm.
Is my hon. friend a statesman now?
Well, I may say that "Hope springs eternal in the human breast."
My hon. friend also probably remembers that "Hope deferred maketh the heart sick."

Well, that may apply to my hon. friend, who is an ex-statesman. I would invite the Minister of Immigration and the Minister of Labour to come to Montreal: I will get together for them a mass meeting of from 4,000 to 5,000 people; we will fill the largest hall in the city. These people will consist altogether of artisans, and the two ministers can get the benefit of their views as to whether there is need in Montreal an I
other large cities for immigration of the class that I have advocated. Many of the departmental officials to whom I have referred are first-class men and I have nothing to say against them, but in other cases dry rot has set in, and when that happens the official is of no possible use to the department; in fact, he is a drag on the wheel. Such people ought to be superannuated or otherwise removed and live persons put in their places who could give the Minister proper information upon these vital matters. The Minister, I understand, is managing five or six different departments; he is doing the best he can, but after all he is only human and he has to take his information from people who are living in the past, who are in the nineteenth century, not in the twentieth; who do not know of conditions in the large cities. How many of them have gone to the large cities and interviewed the artisan classes or the employing classes to find out just what the conditions are? Where they got their information I do not know, but what I do know is that they have made a very sorry fist of it if they have given information to the minister upon which he has based his so-called policy which he brought down to the House this week.
I trust that I may have an opportunity later in the discussion when questions arise out of particular estimates to speak a little further. For the present I should like to have some reply, effective or otherwise, or an attempt even at a reply, to what I think is an arraignment against the department and something which calls for an answer from it.

The hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House (Mr. Jacobs) admitted that he was a voice in the wilderness. He admitted also that he was sniping the government from behind. To alleviate the force of his blow, after a little sniping at his own party he seeks to draw the Canadian Manufacturers' Association into the fray as being in some way connected with the Canada Colonization Association with which this government have made some arrangement. I repudiate that statement absolutely. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association, except as individual citizens, had nothing whatever to do with it.

That is correct. I agree with my hon. friend that it was the members individually of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association who were invited to contribute to the Canada Colonization Association.

I am glad to have that statement from the hon. member because that was the suggestion I took exception to.
That is what he said at the outset.

The hon. member from Nova Scotia might be quiet for a moment. He will have an opportunity later. I would like to put a few questions to the minister regarding this association with which he has made an arrangement, but before doing so I want to emphasize further what I have to say with respect to the organization that has been referred to. I want to read a sentence from a letter of the Canada Colonization Association written within the last two or three months, and you will see then whether the Manufacturers' Association have anything to do with this association and who has to do with it.

My hon. friend referred to the hon. member from Nova Scotia. I will tell him that the hon. member from Nova Scotia represents a free-born constituency and is not a counsel for the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.

I understand, Mr. Chairman, that I have the floor. The sentence I wish to read is as follows. This association speaking of itself, says:
It has the approval and support of the Imperial, federal and provincial governments, the co-operation of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the government-owned railways.
There is no word' there or in this whole letter regarding the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, but there is word of the federal government, and I think the hon. member who has just spoken might take the responsibility himself, as a supporter of this government, when it admits that it has made an arrangement for the payment of public money to this corporation.
In the course of his address the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) told us that this company was without a president. I should like to inquire from the minister who are the officers at present of this association, and would also ask him to give us some further information regarding it. Surely we have a right to know with respect to this company, even if it is a charitable organization, which is good enough for this government to make a contract with of the magnitude it has, what is its personnel and everything regarding it.
