speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Very well.

I admit that my first
words will be to express my sympathy towards the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart). Since he has brought down this policy he has been subjected to criticism not only from both wings of the opposition, but also from behind. I venture to say that if instead of framing his policy he had waited until he was in the House and had heard the different suggestions made to him, and had then tried to put them together, it would have been a tremendous task because I have never yet heard in a debate in this House such a merry-go-round of contradictory statements as have been made here regarding immigration. I will take the stand that even if he has not, as is evident, succeeded in satisfying everyone, yet we should have much sympathy with him in the situation in which he happens to be placed, and understand by the very phases of this debate how complex this problem of immigration is,
An hon. member speaking during the course of this debate stated that the main questions of Canadian politics were the railway question and immigration. Some go further and claim that by increasing population in this country the government will go a long way towards wiping out the railway deficit. It will be

Supply-Immigration
time enough, in my opinion, to deal with that phase of the situation when the railway estimates are before the House, but the problem of immigration in itself suggests so [DOT] many comments that even at the risk of reiterating what has already been said to-day, one feels that one cannot refrain from expressing his own views.
The minister the other day defined the government policy. He stated that in his opinion it was imperative that Canada secure more people. He argued that the financial burden was heavy on the present population, and that increased immigration would lighten it. He also considered it urgent that some selection be made of the immigrants who apply for admission to this country, and he volunteered the opinion that we should not have too many immigrants for the cities on account of the unemployment situation. With that summary statement I will say that personally I find very little fault. The reasons for an increased immigration are perfectly obvious. We live in one of the largest and richest countries in the world. One who travels across this country from ocean to ocean is astonished at the immense possibilities of Canada. It is a country vast as a continent, but its richness lies dormant in the soil beneath for want of the required number of miners, tillers and workers to bring it to light, and if immigration was imperative before the war I contend that it is even more so now under the present conditions.
We have inherited an enormous war debt. In 1896 our net debt was only $225,738,079. In 1911 it had grown to 326 millions and some odd thousands, and in 1922 it stood at $2,366,861,252. In my opinion it has grown at a rate out of all proportion to our population. It is urgent, not only to increase the number of tax payers in this country, but also to increase the production of wealth and the potential paying ability of the community as a whole.
Now, let us look at the figures of our population. From 1911 to 1921 the increase by immigration to this country was 1,975,393. The natural increase in population was 1,836,407, giving what should have been a total increase of 3,811,800 persons. Yet the net increase during that period was only 1,562,851. In other words, as has been stated before, not only did we lose the total number of immigrants that came into Canada during those ten years, but also 273,000 of our natural increase. I will say at once that I am not placing a definite value at all on these figures. I am one who thinks, in common with many others, that the figures of the last census
75i
are not correct. For example, we in Montreal contend that the population of that large city has been underrated by the census figures to the extent of fully 100,000 people. But taking the facts as they are, it is very clear that we need more immigrants if we hope to maintain our population at the figure at which it should stand.
Some say-it has been said in this debate- that we need not spend any money on immigration because all the immigrants we induce to come to Canada leave us, and therefore the money is misspent. But we have no proof at all, Mr. Chairman, that the 1,800,000 people who left us during the ten year period referred to had been immigrants. On the con-traiy, I claim that if we had had no immigration at all during those ten years the conditions that brought about the exodus from this country to the States would have had their effect to a certain degree, and instead of reporting an increase in population-however small it may look to us-we would probably have had a decrease. And touching this subject I will say, that although I have much sympathy in theory with the efforts made towards repatriation I do not entertain any great hope that that phase of the government's policy, even with the co-operation of the provinces, will have very much effect. I think it is much harder to entice any citizen to come back to this country than to prevent him from leaving, or than to replace him by another citizen through the medium of immigration. Therefore I think it is obvious- and we might in the confusion of opinions expressed in the course of this debate agree, at least, on this point-that we should try, in some way, to increase the number of our immigrants. But it is also true that we must exercise some care in their selection.
As to the country of origin let me say very frankly that this, to my mind, is of much less importance, than the character of the individual immigrant. We may get good settlers and we may get bad settlers from any country on the earth. It is quite natural that we should try to secure a large number of immigrants from the British Isles. It would also be natural for us to try to secure a number of immigrants from France and Belgium. Here let me say that it is very hard to get any immigrants at all from either of the last two countries mentioned. It is well known that even in normal times Frenchmen do not emigrate to other countries, that they are very strongly attached to their native land. If that is true in normal times, how much more true must it be in this period of after war reconstruction. The French government itself is very anxious at this moment to keep its
Supply-Immigration

French children on the soil of France in order that the efforts towards reconstruction be brought to their full fruition. Furthermore, we all know that there is a decrease of population in France due to the falling off in births, and that there were very heavy losses during the war. It is also well known that any immigration propaganda in
5 p.m. France is prohibited by the govern-of the republic. Such propaganda was barely tolerated before the war; now it is very strictly prohibited. Therefore, I would like to state, in all frankness, that although we are very desirous of securing settlers from France and Belgium, it would appear to be a very hard task, and for my part I would not feel inclined to blame the government too severely if the stream of immigration from these two countries does not flow to Canada more copiously than it does at present.
Do I understand that the laws of Belgium prohibit emigration from that country now?

I was alluding more particularly to France. I will frankly admit that I am not positive as to what is taking place in Belgium. I am inclined to think, however, that it would be somewhat easier to procure immigrants from the latter conutry, more especially in view of the fact that the population of Belgium is very dense. Nevertheless, it is a fact that it has always been very hard to attract immigrants from both these countries.
There is a large number of Belgians in the West.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That immigration is under government supervision.

I frankly admit, for I believe in being frank about these matters, that I have much sympathy with the proposal made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St George (Mr. Marler) as regards immigrants from those countries with which we were at war during the great conflict. Such immigration, however, must be under regulation; we must be very careful in admitting such immigrants to this country. Again I say I have no prejudice at all against immigrants coming from any country in the world; I attach much more importance to the character of the individual than I do to the country of origin.
As regards the question of regulations, I will not go into it fully as my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) has done. Nor will I say that I endorse all that that hon. member has said. But I would
(Mr. Rinfret.]
suggest, in a general way, that the regulations be made less rigid in their application, and that the authorities use some discretion in regard to individual cases. I place little faith in any stringent rule which is not intelligently applied and carried out with discretion.
I must say also that I was much surprised, during the course of the debate, to hear so many hon. members opposite object to the immigration of farmers and farm help. I think they are the very immigrants that we do require and that there is unlimited space for them in Canada. The average farmer succeeds very easily in feeding and maintaining his family. The exodus from the rural parts of Canada is not due, in my opinion, to inability to secure subsistence; it is due to the lure of the city, which exerts its influence on well off and very prosperous far-, mers.
Does my hon. friend suggest that all the incoming immigrants require is space?

They require space where they can get busy, where they can live and subsist. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) just a moment ago read a report of a sitting of the legislature at Toronto, which report, in his opinion, went to show that we needed immigrants in the city and that we did not need them on the farms. Yet what did he read, but simply this, that farmers in Ontario were all asking for help? He was blaming 'the men in the cities who needed work for not going on to those farms to help those Ontario farmers; I think every line of the report that he read was ample proof that, in that part of the country at least, if men were needed, they were needed as farm help by Ontario farmers. I am not so sure that we need immigrants in the cities. It is all very well to say that at present there is little unemployment and that most people who really care to work can find work. I know very well that some people will refuse work under any conditions. I will also agree that others will claim that they are entitled to work according to their willingness and taste, their own opinion as to what should be their standard of living; but I claim there are to-day, especially in large cities, quite a number of men who cam not find any employment whatever. We have heard the hon. member for St. Lawrence^ St. George, for whom I have great respect, venture an opinion somewhat in opposition to that, and the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier has said the same thing. I should like to agree with them. Perhaps we

Supply-Immigra tion
may agree on this point. Every Saturday morning when I am in my office in Montreal,
I have about a hundred callers asking for work. If the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George or the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier will tell me where I can send those men, I shall be very grateful to him. In agreement with the government policy, I would strongly object to any immigration effort which would tend to increase the number of unemployed in. the large cities of Canada. We want immigrants for the farms; but we have an over supply of population in the cities, and the very fact that there is a tendency to leave the farm for the city is no proof at all that the policy is wrong. On the contrary, does it not show that we should do our utmost to send as many men as we can to the farms and to restrict a3 many as we can from entering the cities?
How is the hon. member going to prevent them from entering the cities?

I agree with the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier when he says that you cannot prevent nature from following its course; but I think by taking the necessary precaution to ensure that any immigrant coming into this country is a farmer or has farming aspirations, we shall go some distance towards that goal. The fact that something is hard to prevent, is no argument at all that we should not attempt to prevent it. It is, on the contrary, ample argument that we should have a policy that will do the utmost to secure that result.
My hon. friend will, perhaps, remember that I said I agreed with assisted immigration as regards agriculture, but I would allow immigrants who present themselves voluntarily to come to the cities.

I agree with that. I think my hon. friend is closer to my views than some hon. members opposite, and I am glad to record that.
The minister says that he intends to spend money in advertising this country and letting everyone know of its great possibilities. That is very sound and to that I do not object. But he also intends to spend pretty large sums of money with special organizations whose business it is to secure immigrants. He has contracted with the Canada Colonization Association for ten months at a figure of 8100,000, provided that they procure a minimum of 200 families during the ten months. I believe that is their proposal. Taking the average family at five, which I believe is a reasonable
figure, that will mean a minimum of a thousand settlers who will cost this country a hundred dollars per head. That is paying a very high price, and unless the minister is able to get a much larger number than the minimum stated, he is hardly getting a commensurate return for the money spent.
There is another proposal to spend $600,000 in connection with the British Empire Settlement Board. I understand that board has been working in connection with the Australian government, and while the reports that I have read may not be accurate-I say again you get reports on this matter which are very contradictory-I do not see that the results have been very favourable in Australia. The immigrants which this board has been able to send to Australia have been moderate in numbers and rather low in quality. I believe in attracting immigrants in the ordinary 'way, but the amount seems very large.
What number does the hon. member say that Australia got?

I have not that before me.
I was speaking in a general way.
What is the hon. gentleman's information as to the morale of the immigrants which Australia got?
Perhaps the hon. gentleman, when he speaks in this debate, will discuss that point.
My hon. friend made an assertion.

I think I qualified the statement. I do not object altogether to the large sum of money; but it should not be spent unless we are sure of having good results. I have quite a large amount of confidence in the present government. If I were sitting on the other side of the room, I would probably be more inclined to be cautious. But I am voicing the opinion in a general way regarding the Settlement Board and the Colonization Association, that this is not the best way to secure immigrants for this country.

Does my hon. friend know who are the members of this company with which he alleges a contract has been entered into by the government? If it is Sir John Willison who is connected with it, I do not wonder at the hon. member's doubting.

The Settlement Board or the other company?
Supply-Immigration
The company with which a contract was entered into on the basis of 200 families.
That is the Canada Colonization Association.
Who are the members of it?

I do not know. The government has contracted with the company at a certain figure. I am giving my opinion as to the principle of any such contract, no matter who are the members of such a company. I say, in a general way, whether it be the Settlement Board or the Colonization Company, I take little stock in the work of any such company which indulges in wholesale bargaining for immigrants at a certain figure, for a certain consideration, whether their idea be to get paid for the work they do, or to free another country from a certain surplus of population that they do not want, but that they would like us to absorb. I think that the immigrant who is attracted to this country because he thinks the place is worth while, and comes of his own will, is on the average a better prospect than any immigrant who has been influenced and attracted into the country by companies whose interests are merely to live up to a contract, or who possibly are engaged in relieving other countries of an overflow of population.
I would direct the attention of the minister to this more especially, and ask him if he is going to apply his regulations at all rigidly- to be much more stringent with any flow of immigrants sent out at so much per head by any settlement board or company than with the average immigrant who comes on his own responsibility because he has discovered that Canada will very likely prove a fine country for him to live in.
No matter where these immigrants may come from, I say that we should see to it that they shall become good Canadians. What is assimilation?-asked an hon. member during the course of the debate on this question. Centuries ago a Roman pro-consul put a similar question to the multitude: "What is truth?" Now, we all know what assimilation is; we all know what the word means. It means not only that a person coming into this country should be able to speak or should learn one of the current languages of the country, but it also implies the obligation to interest himself in the country's general welfare and become a part of its social and economic life. Any body of immigrants, call them Doukhobors, Mennonites, or by any other name you choose, who retain their 
peculiar class identity after their arrival in this country and who continue to lead a separate and distinct life from the great Canadian body, falls short, in my opinion, of all that is implied in the term "assimilation." Differences, racial or otherwise, are numerous enough in this country without our adding to their number.
Now, it is often charged that hon. members' utterances on this subject lack consistency and preciseness. Quite a number of questions have been put to every speaker, questions very kindly in their phraseology; and I have done my best to answer such questions. Some, I admit, I could not answer. Possibly that has detracted somewhat from the logical sequence of my speech; and it might have been more advantageous to a proper conclusion of my remarks had I been allowed to travel a continuous and uninterrupted route. However, before I resume my seat I should like to sum up my remarks briefly. We need immigrants, but we should not pay too high a price for them. We need them on the farms and not in the cities; and they should be subject to regulations moderately and discreetly enforced. We should advertise this country, too, as well as improve its living conditions, so as to retain within its borders the citizens we already have. In the expenditure in connection with the Canada Colonization Association and the Empire Settlement Board, I have little faith; and I trust that the government will promptly discontinue such expenditure if it fails to bring proper- and unexpected-results.

Most of us appreciate the
courage displayed by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) in attacking members of his own party, and particularly the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart). But I was not very deeply impressed with the policy which the hon. gentleman would substitute for that offered by the minister. I think the hon. member went out of his way a good deal to find justification for a criticism of labour in Canada, and he characterized the policy of the Minister of Immigration as a watertight compartment.
I am sorry I cannot say as much for his policy; in fact, it was leaking all over. I wish to show in a few sentences how he misrepresented the policy of labour with regard to immigration.
If I understood the policy as outlined by the minister and by those who have supported him, I should say it seeks by immigration, fir^t, to reduce taxation, secondly, to increase production, and in the third place to bring prosperity out of the economic chaos in which

Supply-I mmigration
we find ourselves at the present time. We all agree that these are noble purposes; the intentions back of them are very good; and I think we shall have to extend our sympathy not only to the minister himself but to the Cabinet as well in dealing with the situation that faces Canada to-day. We fully realize that the government did not create these economic conditions which they seek to alleviate through an immigration policy; we frankly admit that they are not responsible for them in any way andi that they cannot materially affect them by legislation at this time. We must recognize their problem as one that calls for the consideration not only of the Cabinet, or of the minister or of any party, but of parliament and of the people of Canada as well. The government are in a wilderness of . economic difficulties to-day, no doubt because of following to some extent what I would call a vague and unanalyzed tradition.
It has been stated by some of the speakers that have been supporting the policy of the minister that, following the assumption of power by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Canada experienced a great period of prosperity; and it is assumed that, by continuing an immigration policy similar to that which was in force during the regime of the late right hon. gentleman, a corresponding prosperity will ensue. Now, there have been periods of prosperity so-called and periods of depression. These alternate; and a period of depression is simply a sign of the coming prosperity, and vice versa. But prosperity does not come merely because an immigration policy of any kind is in force. It is not detracting in any respect from the greatness of Sir Wilfrid Laurier to say that his immigration policy was not what constituted the prosperity attributed to his regime. There are many economic factors that enter into these cycles of prosperity. There is such a thing as a world situation to be considered, where the producers of a country can find a market for their produce. There is manipulation of credit, by those who control the financial system of a country; there is inflation as well as deflation of credit, reflecting itself in high prices or in a slump in prices, as the case may be. Then there are favourable crop conditions, and hundreds of other circumstances to be taken into consideration. So that we must not assume, merely because prosperity happened to obtain during a certain political regime in Canada, in which an immigration policy was fostered, that we shall therefore usher in again a similarly prosperous period by the adoption of another immigration policy of the same kind.
I submit that there is no connection between an immigration policy and prosperity, except that prosperity may attract immigrants whereas immigrants do not necessarily bring prosperity in their wake. The government are evidently aware of the unfavourable economic conditions that prevail, and have attempted >
to bring forward an immigration policy by which in part they seek to remedy these conditions. The government are conscious of enemies of the state as for instance unemployment, high prices of commodities, high taxation, and an enormous national debt-these enemies are besetting the nation, and the government is striking at them. I think it is striking in the dark, assisted ably by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs).
Now, it is all very well for us to criticize, and I think most of the criticisms we have listened to so far have not contained much of constructive value. I purpose to advance the ideas of labour with regard to immigration, and I hope that the government will at least listen to my suggestions, if they do not follow them in detail. I scarcely anticipate that the hon. Minister of Immigration will adopt the policy of labour in toto, but I do hope that he will give it consideration. Speaking for myself, and attempting as best I can to interpret the opinions of labour on immigration, I want to state that they are not opposed to immigration. The attack made by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) would lead the House to believe that the policy of Labour in this country was opposed to every kind of immigration under all circumstances. It is true that we oppose certain policies of immigration that do not make for permanency, policies which do not take proper care of immigrants after arrival, policies which have been inaugurated with an absolute disregard of conditions prevailing at the time. These are the reasons for our opposing immigration on certain occasions, but our opposition is not to be regarded as permanent.
That all hired labour outside of Canada must be secured through the employment service of Canada is one of the requirements which the labour organizations of this country demand from the Minister of Immigration. And it is not difficult to see why they should urge this requirement. I understand that last year certain companies in this country requested that several thousands of miners be immediately shipped in from Belgium to work our coal mines. That request was investigated by a certain organization in this country, and it was discovered that there were already enough miners here to take care of all our
Supply-Immigration

requirements; in fact there were more than were necessary to operate our coal mines. In such circumstances it surely would have been folly to bring from Belgium a thousand or more miners who had specialized in that particular line, and thereby less fitted by that very specialization to take up other vocations, even if opportunities offered themselves. That is one reason why Labour is opposed to certain policies of immigration under certain conditions.
We want an immigration policy that', first of all, will contain in itself the elements of permanency when put into operation. Much emphasis has already been laid upon the fact that Canada is an immigration sieve, that we take in immigrants on one side and drop them out on the other, that we are losing to the United States and perhaps to some other countries more immigrants than we take in, notwithstanding the expenditure which has been made to attract them here. The problem for Canada, according to the Labour view, is not so much one of immigration as one of emigration and colonization. How, then, do we propose to colonize? Here are a few suggestions which I would submit for the consideration of the minister dealing with this question.
First, I submit that a colonization scheme should be devised to settle our vacant lands close to railroads. That immediately brings us face to face with the high price of lands. How are we going to settle immigrants who come here with very little money on lands that are close to railways? These are the high-priced lands, the lands that, somehow or other, have been secured by favoured individuals in this country. The minister said that he thought approximately $1,500 would be a very fair beginning for an immigrant to settle upon the land. How far would $1,500 go in purchasing land valued at the lowest possible price at $20 per acre, some of it as high as $50 per acre very near a railroad? How is that immigrant going to begin with $1,500 to pay high interest charges on his purchase, to equip himself with the implements necessary for farming, and to feed himself for at least a year? I tell you what would happen-

I would ask my hon. friend, why should the taxpayers of -Canada pay one cent to any person to come into this country? If people want to come, let them come so long as they are not physically unfit or Bolshevist. It is better to keep one good Canadian here than to bring in fifteen hundred foreigners.
fMr. Irvine.]

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has stated my position about as clearly as I could state it myself. I am not advocating that we pay money to bring people to this country. I am trying to show, as the basis of my opposition to the present immigration policy that after paying money to bring them in we cannot keep them here.
We should not pay anything.

What will happen with a $1,500 beginning is that the immigrant will have to look for work in the city to pay the interest charges on the farm which he will never be able to own. Fifteen hundred dollars will not go very far in purchasing land. So some scheme must be found to free our land for the use, first of all, of the people who are here now landless; and secondly, for those who may subsequently be brought in. In pursuing this idea we should have an examination of all lands listed, and there should next take place an expropriation of all lands held at unreasonable prices. I have used the term "expropriation." Let me modify that and say, let us tax that land in order to free it. Such a procedure will increase the revenue of the country, while at the same time forcing the land from the hands of the exploiter and into the hands of those whom we are bringing into this country to increase production.
In the next place, we request that assistance should be given for the building of farm homes either to the labourers on the farms that we propose to bring in or to the fanners themselves.
Now, it may be asked: Whom should we first colonize; when lands have become available? In answer to that question-assuming of course that we are going to introduce single tax and free the land quickly-I submit it as a reasonable proposition that it is better for us to begin to colonize the people who are already in Canada than to go outside for others while our own people are walking the streets. If we cannot colonize the people that we already have, by what process of reasoning does the Minister of Immigration presume to be able to colonize new comers? That is a question which I should like him to answer when he replies to all the tirades of criticism to which his policy has already been subjected. If, then, it be a sane and good policy to put people on the land, we want first of all to colonize our land with the people already here, those in the unemployed ranks at the present time, and those who may be employed but who would rather go on the land if they saw an

opportunity of making a living there. I am not going to deal with farming conditions. These, I presume, will be dealt with by the hon. members representing the farming interests of this country, and dealt with well, I have no doubt.
Colonization opportunities, I insist, should first be offered to all residents in Canada, and the employment service offices should be used as recruiting offices in this connection. Let me for a moment in this respect refer to the child immigration policy of the Minister of Immigration. I think he proposes to encourage the bringing in from other countries of children somewhere around the age of fourteen years. I may not be quite correct in stating that age. However, let me point out what happens to the children of Canada, and ask the minister if we should not try by some means to keep our own children alive before we begin to import others from outside countries. The number of children who died in the respective provinces last year before they were a year old was as follows: Prince Edward Island, 180; Nova Scotia, 1,311; New Brunswick, 1,299; Ontario, 6,763; Manitoba, 1,533; Saskatchewan, 1,814; Alberta, 1,391; British Columbia, 602; Quebec, 11,389. This is an enormous death rate among children, yet we are to go over to Great Britain or elsewhere and bring in others.	It is true that those
we intend to bring in are older than those referred to in these statistics, but if we could keep this large number of children alive they would make far better citizens than any children we could bring in, even if we went to Scotland for them. It was recently found in Alberta, the great farming country that is to be laid open for these immigrants, that 1,500 children were suffering from malnutrition. If we cannot feed our own children now; if we cannot keep alive the children we have brought to life in this country, why should we seek to bring others in from other countries ?
I understand that it is the law in Ontario that children shall go to school until they are sixteen. Does the minister want to bring in children at the age of fourteen and put them to work-that is what I call cheap labour- with farmers, thus violating or helping to violate the law of the province and lowering the educational standard of the community? If not, what provision is he going to make that these young boys and girls coming from Great Britain, leaving the opportunity of getting an education there, shall, in spite of doing chores and becoming the servants of farmers, have an opportunity at least to get as good an education as they would have got had they
stayed in their native country;-indeed, as good as any other child in Canada gets under the present law?

I am glad that the sentiments I" wish to express are echoed from the government side. I shall come to the advertising in a few moments; for the present I am trying to submit a constructive policy embodying the expressed opinions of organized labour in regard to immigration.
We believe that some organization should handle the colonization scheme that I have suggested. I would add to that suggestion that the Soldier Settlement Board or some similarly qualified organization should be charged with the work of surveying and reporting upon available lands for settlement in all parts of the Dominion, keeping in view the fact that it is our own people we first want to colonize. If we succeed in doing that, it will be a good argument for the getting of more people to colonize. All this might be summarized .in that well known and well worn phrase, "Back to the land." Getting back to the land ought to begin here; if we follow some such scheme of colonization as I have suggested and get our own people on the land, we will not need to advertise for others to come in from outside.
Our manufacturers to-day are highly protected, on the ground, as they say, that they are infant industries, and so on, and that they want to be sure that their investments are safeguarded. All that labour is asking in regard to immigration policy is that their interests may be, not protected, but given some consideration. Labour desires that it shall have the right to live, not that it shall be degraded and destroyed by any immigration policy whatsoever. If the Canadian Manufacturers' Association can claim protection from this parliament for their machinery and their investments, it is surely fair and reasonable that labour should ask parliament not to advocate or advance a policy that would imperil the rights of labour to get

My hon. friend, being closer to the Minister of Immigration, is in a better position to answer that question than I am. I am certainly not asking for any selection of

immigrants, but I am saying that from such an advertisement as I have quoted, it is not likely we shall have any great rush, and if we have no great rush of immigrants to this country we shall not have the resultant difficulties we have had during the last few years. I want to finish this quotation to show that South Africa has taken a different course with regard to advertising from that which we have followed in Canada:
This is being increasingly realized; the stream of migrants to the union of South Africa is comparatively small, but it is select and continuous.
The people who in recent years have gone to the union of South Africa are people not only of means but of judgment. They went only after weighing the prospect. What satisfied them may merit investigation by you. Is it not worth looking into?
Now if South Africa is getting the immigrants that have judgment and capital, I submit that in view of the present economic conditions in Canada the only immigrants we could hope to get would be those without judgment, and I do not think it would be good policy for us to spend $200,000 or more in trying to get into this country immigrants who have no judgment.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say frankly that I rise to oppose the minister's immigration policy. My great objection, of course, to the minister's policy is his endorsation of the Canada Colonization Association. I am very sorry that the minister has apparently taken a place in this great national colonization scheme that is lower than that taken by the Colonization Association. I had hoped that at least he would be the leading figure, the chief authority in the whole matter. I have an article here that was released for evening papers Winnipeg and west of Winnipeg, Monday, September 11, 1922, and also for morning and evening papers east of Winnipeg, September 11. It starts as follows:
The Western Ca*nada Colonization Association, in close co-operation with the federal and Imperial governments and the Canadian railways have worked out a well matured land settlement policy, which is to be put into effect forthwith.
That in the first place is my objection to this whole scheme. The date of announcing this policy was in September of last year. Just about that time we had harvested one of the largest crops that had ever been grown and matured in Canada, and it seems to me, reading between the lines and considering the whole question, that the people who were interested in this scheme remembered the good times we had in Canada as a result of the crop of 1915. I remember reading how in southern Alberta the farmers went to various loan company officials who refused to

Supply-Immigration
accept payment of mortgages in full. Possibly in this case the Canada Colonization Assoeia-toin was expecting a return of that sort of prosperity and was ready to climb on to the band wagon. At least, that is the impression I have received from reading their literature and putting that together with the date of the announcement of the policy. However, " the best-laid schemes o' mice an' men gang aft agley," and it must have been so in this case. We have not had a return, of prosperity since the tremendous crop that was grown and matured in western Canada last year. In fact, I doubt if the country is as well off on the whole as it was one year before.
I want to examine further the manifesto of this association. In the leading paragraph we have the problem and the solution stated, as follows:
The British and Canadian governments have joined with the Canada Colonization Association and the Canadian railways in a co-ordinated land settlement plan covering all the provinces. An efficient colonization machine is being set up and will begin to operate forthwith. Colonization in Canada has been at a comparative standstill ever since 1913. Yet nothing is clearer than that effective land settlement on a comprehensive scale is the only available solution of the country's pressing economic and financial problems. By increasing the farming population and agricultural production throughout Canada, we shall lower freight rates, stimulate business, lighten the burden of the national debt to every individual family, lessen federal, provincial, and municipal taxation, and go far to eliminate the seflous annual deficit on the National Railways.
The scope of the plan is comprehensive enough. It promises a great deal, promises what no group of men anywhere can guarantee. The first promise it makes is that it will bring back prosperity. That is a very general statement.
It is also claimed that it will lower freight rates. Now anyone who studies the question of freight rates in Canada during the last ten years will, I think, come to the conclusion that increased population does not necessarily mean lower freight rates. Of course, there may be circumstances to take into consideration; the circumstances during the next ten years may be altogether different from those during the last ten years.

Can the hon. member
tell me who is the Deputy Minister of Immigration and where he is at the present time?

No, I have
not been investigating that matter. This national scheme of land settlement, presided over and controlled very largely by the Canada Colonization Association, according to this manifesto promises a great deal. Some of the things that it promises will, I think, be fulfilled, but considering all the statements made
in this manifesto I think it shows a great lack of real consideration for the welfare of the intending immigrant.
I have no objection, in fact, I am very anxious like any other Canadian to see our railways prosper, and the country as a whole, but unless we give the intending immigrant every consideration, and a great deal more than he will obtain under this land settlement plan, we can never have an ultimately successful immigration policy. The first thing we learn, according to this manifesto, that the settler is going to do is to lighten our burden of debt. That means that the settler will have to assume a certain portion of our national debt when he comes into Canada as a settler. Though I am not a prophet, and have never professed to be, I would not mind guaranteeing that that promise regarding the incoming settler will be absolutely fulfilled regardless of what government or governments may be in power for the next ten or fifty years.
Regarding the lowering of freight rates, I do not think we have any real justification at the present time for saying that the mere incoming of immigrants will lower freight rates.
Will the hon. member not admit that if the railways get increased traffic they will have greater earnings, and that consequently we may ask for a reduction in freight rates?
(Edmonton): That is a different thing from what the Canada Colonization Association is preaching in this manifesto.
I asked the hon. member a question. Does he not admit that?

That it is possible? Yes. I certainly do. I wonder if the benefits that are supposed to accrue to the people of Canada, or to the people who are already here are passed on, or if the intending immigrants are informed as to both sides of this question. I remember in the Highlands of Scotland, away back in the year 1900 and a few years following, the very roseate literature that we used to get on immigration. I remember that on the front page of these pamphlets there would be a picture of a tar-paper shack, and two or three pages further on an illustration of an experimental farm and generally, beneath the picture was written "After a few years." Of course, railways and other conveniences found mention. I believe, however, notwithstanding the literature issued in the Old Land by the Department of Immigration that the works of Ralph Connor exercised the greatest force in interesting the people. I want to say further that

in any literature sent abroad, either by the government or by this or any other like association, the effort should be to tell the truth as nearly as possible, and not seek to create a false impression. When the advantages which may accrue to settlers coming to Canada are dilated on there ought to be, side by side with that statement, some account given of the disadvantages which the new arrivals will have to face.
The men who were behind the present scheme when it was announced-and I suppose that their spirit controls its operations even at present, at any rate to some extent- were not farmers, and yet they were associated in a movement to induce farmers to settle on the lands of western Canada. The president of the association at that time was Sir John Willison who has written a book entitled Reminiscences, Political and Personal. Now on page 10 of that work we find the following:
But one may love the woods and the fields and not like farming. I got away from the farm as soon as I could, and I have not wanted to return. Nor have I ever heard that there was any desire that I should. It is often said that a good farmer has been spoiled to make a poor lawyer or a poor doctor. Whether or not I am a good journalist, no one who knows will suggest that I was likely to become a good farmer. The fashion changes. It is a sure word of prophecy that the movement towards the cities has spent itself. Moving pictures, rural mail delivery, good roads, motors, bath-rooms, house furnaces, and many other devices to save labour, enhance comfort and relieve isolation, make the country ever more desirable, and better prices give the farmers an increasing but still inadequate return for their labour. In a democracy rooted in the soil lies the sanity and stability of human institutions. But we cannot all be farm?rs, and to many of us a call comes that will not be denied. Whether we go to town or country, still blessed is he that findeth himself.

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee rose at six o'clock, I was dealing with this national land settlement plan as advertised in the western papers on September 11. The plan is, according to the language of the advertisement, to drum up settlers in the United States and also in Great Britain, though I understand the association is not operating in Great Britain at the present time, to bring them to Canada and to settle them on the land. The first thing that must be ascertained with regard to a settler is whether he has enough cash to start on a quarter section of land. He is to be settled on unoccupied land. The vast majority of such settlers will, of course, come from parts of

the country which have been fairly well developed, where they have bams, houses, fences, water supply and other necessary things for the successful operation of a farm. To take men of that type with what little stock they may bring along with them, to place them on unoccupied quarter sections and to ask them there to make a payment of two dollars an acre and to sign an agreement that they will pay the balance in thirty-two years with interest at 6 per cent, even though under the agreement they have not to pay any principal for the first two years, is something of a problem.
The weakness in that scheme lies in this. Supposing a settler comes from some one of the fairly well-developed western states to Canada, and buys land on the recommendation of the association or any officer of the government. He can hardly be said to be doing that of his own initiative. From my knowledge of farming and of the real estate business in general, as it has been and is 'being carried on in western Canada, I think more mistakes have been made through men buying farms or lots pn the recommendation of others, be they real estate agents or otherwise, than in any other way, and this has been a great detriment to the country. To bring settlers in from the United States, regardless of the organization that is instrumental in bringing them in, or from Great Britain, should any come from there, and avail themselves of the services of this Canada Colonization Association, and to tie them down, or as Sir John Willison says, to get them rooted on the land with an initial payment of $2 an acre and an agreement to pay the balance in thirty-two years, before they have had time to become fairly well acquainted with the seasons and the general conditions prevailing in the country is, to my mind, a big undertaking and one of the principal weaknesses in this scheme.
Life on the farm in western Canada, especially, is a life of loneliness in many cases, and if there is one thing above everything else a settler needs, if he is to make good, it is self-reliance and personal initiative. If settlers are brought into this country by a shepherding organization, many settlers will very likely be brought in who would not on their own personal initiative have come in, and the result will be, I am afraid, that we shall have a larger percentage of failures under this scheme than possibly we could have had under any other plan. I came to this country something like twenty years ago; I have gone through the various stages of homesteading and so on, and my experience has

Supply-Immigration
been that the easiest thing in all those twenty years was to emigrate and that the hard experiences came afterwards. If we are going to settle 15,000,000 acres in western Canada under this system, I am afraid we shall have a very much larger percentage of discontented settlers than we have at the present time. It is much easier for a settler to become discontented and it is much more likely that he will become discontented under this plan under which he is advised to buy land by an organization such as this, than if he came of his own initiative and took up land because he wanted that land and because he was led to want it through his experience in and knowledge of the country.
We are advised further that this association, through its officers, is going to set up what it calls "community clubs," which, apparently, are going to look after those settlers after they come to Canada in order that they may not drift to the cities. It will be very difficult to prevent them from doing that, and that phase of the operations of the organization is practically worthless. After the settlers have been established in communities and they have those local community clubs organized, I find in this circular what the clubs will do:
(a)	prepare a chart of its particular district which will indicate occupied and unoccupied farms.
And so on.
(b)	assist the officials of the Canada Colonization Association in securing listings of land.
(c)	Report on vacant lands and land valuations in each district.
Apparently, after these community clubs are established in various districts, they are going to be used to further the interests of the Canada Colonization' Association.
(d)	Induce local farmers to write their friends "back home," advising them of the advantageous opportunities for land settlement in their neighbourhoods.
I am afraid we have in this something that might become a rather dangerous principle. The settler pays his $2 per acre down in the first place, and then he signs an agreement to pay the balance in thirty-two annual payments with interest at 6 per cent. After he pays down his initial $2 per acre, he gets two years without paying any principal; but I am afraid that to take hold of a raw quarter section and to grow anything more than feed for stock during those two years, will be more than the average settler can do. Although the ordinary farmer is not a man who is very ready with his pen or fond of writing letters, it is possible that some of them might be induced, through a promise of an extension of time on some payment that might be overdue, to rvrite to their friends back home. I
am afraid we are being asked to endorse something that is not in the best interest of the settlers who might come to this country through the agency of the Canada Colonization Association.
It is stated that the landowner will pay the Canada Colonization Association $2 per acre. There may be some dispute in regard to this. This manifesto would indicate that the owners of vacant lands would pay the association $2 commission. It is open to dispute, however, as to just who will pay that $2. It may be that conditions will be such that land cannot be raised in value an extra 82 to meet that commission; but from a knowledge of real estate practices in the country I am afraid there is a chance that in a great many cases this is what will be done. We have not solved the problem for the settlers in bringing them in in this way; and I will go further and say that encouraging settlers to come in this manner, who would not otherwise be likely to come, is not a very good guarantee for their future success as farmers, at least in western Canada.
There are others, however, who are going to benefit from this organization. Thousands of absentee owners of unoccupied lands along the railways are tired of paying heavy taxes and super taxes on these unproductive holdings and would gladly dispose of their property at prices and on terms that would facilitate purchase by incoming settlers. The absentee landowners will be benefited. I also find that the American as well as the local land men will be provided with business. I find here that the former Minister of Agriculture of the province of Alberta will shortly tour the British Isles speaking in support of British agricultural emigratidn to lands in Canada. The statement is made, too, that others will be employed by the Dominion government and the association in an endeavour to work up this great land settlement plan. The association, it is said, has a subscribed capita! of $1,500,000. It does not show in this manifesto how much of this has been actually paid up. So far, I do not know; and I am wondering whether anything more has been paid in in cash than has come from the federal treasury. The expectation of the officers in charge of the organization is that between $30,000,000 and $40,000,000 will be earned in commissions in the next ten years, to be disbursed in the working out of this plan; and it is further stated that the plan is non-profit sharing. Well, there are various ways of sharing profits, and I think that profits are often paid in salaries. And, of course, if they are paid in salaries and good salaries in some cases, dividends may

A good deal has been said about the value of British and American immigrants to Canada. We have been given to understand a great many times, not only on the floor of this House but also in agricultural papers throughout the country, and from other sources, that these settlers could bring to us a knowledge of intensive farming which we need very much in Canada. I do not quite agree with that view. I believe that we do need a little more intensive rather than extensive farming in Canada; but I do not believe that the new settlers coming in from the United States or Great Britain are the people that are going to show us how to carry on this farming. I believe that the demonstration is more likely to come from the men who have been through the mill in the past few years of our country's history and who know the mistakes that may have been made. What are the conditions on farms in the Old Land? On farms of 100 acres there you have good fences, good stone buildings, and every convenience at hand. You will find possibly five persons on such a farm besides the tenant, who generally goes around managing the business. Who could not farm intensively under such conditions? Do you think settlers coming from the Old Country are going to apply those same intensive conditions here, where one man would have to tackle a whole quarter section himself, in addition to building fences, herding stock and putting up his buildings, possibly all at the same time? That is a different matter. The Old Country settler coming out here and settling on land under this plan might find, after he had done his day's work, that he had no good pasture to put his stock in for the first summer, and he might be driven to the necessity of merely hobbling his horses and turning them out at night while he rolled himself under his tent or retired into his cabin, whichever he might happen to have, in the hope that Providence might be kind enough not to allow the mosquitoes to drive them away before morning.
.Does the hon. member approve, or does he not, of inviting British settlers, agriculturists, to come here?
I approve of inviting British settlers to come, but not under this plan, which would place them on the land before they had any knowledge of the country.
Would it be impertinent to ask the hon. gentleman whether he could suggest a better method of getting them here?
Just allow them to come; they will come if conditions are fairly reasonable.
That does not answer my question.
Let the hon. member state his question again.

Under what conditions
would my hon. friend suggest inviting settlers to come here if they are not competent to take up farming of this description?

Let us inform these people just how conditions are here. We have immigration agencies in the Old Land. I suppose there are still immigration agents in Glasgow, Edinburgh, London and such places, and they could give the people a fair knowledge of the facts, placing before them both sides of the situation. They could come if they wished, and I think there would come as many as we can assimilate and settle under present conditions. But when you undertake to drum them up, according to the language of this pamphlet, you have a different problem altogether on your hands.
I am very much interested in this question of immigration, and nothwithstanding anything I may have said against this plan, I am in favour of seeing a reasonable number of immigrants come to this country. But I am opposed to this plan because I think we are putting the cart before the horse; we have not finished with the colonization plans we have had under way for the last number of years, in the West at any rate. The most recent undertaking of this kind was the soldier settlement scheme. I happen to represent a constituency that possibly has the largest block of land settled in the last ten years-I refer to West Edmonton as the constituency and the Peace River country as the settlement. We have in that country Britishers, Americans, French Canadians, Germans, Russians, Hungarians and all the other nationalities now represented in Canada. And I want to say to hon. gentlemen that I do not see very much difference in all those settlers. As one hon. member said this afternoon, it is not so much a question of nationality as of character; there are good and bad people in all nationalities. But those settlers are having a hard time. There is a large German settlement in the Peace River country. I must say that they are very good settlers, and they were good citizens during the war.

Supply-Immigration
What about the other settlers, were they good citizens, too, during the war?

Yes. These German settlers have had an agent in Mexico lately to see what the prospects are down there, because they have been so greatly disappointed in the railway facilities promised them and which they require so urgently. From 1918 on a large number of soldier settlers came into the Peace River country. They took up homesteads, of course, back from the original centres of settlement. In 1910, 1911 and 1912 the good clean prairie land was picked up, and a great many of the soldier settlers are back on the poplar-covered land.
I do not tlynk we have yet done our duty by the settlers in this country. A great many of them who came in from the United States have informed me that wherever they went during the years previous to 1911 and 1912 they were met by immigration agents of the various railway companies advertising the country and describing the proposed railroad through to the Pacific coast, and inducing them to come in in the belief that before they got well established all those railway facilities would be provided.
Now, I suppose it may strike some hon. members that the Peace River country is so far away that we should not use it as an example. But we have settlers also in West Edmonton who are located right along both sides of the Grand Trunk Pacific and that branch of the Canadian National Railways running northwest from the city of Edmonton, and among these settlers are many ex-soldiers. It may surprise the committee to be informed that settlers in the Peace River country are just as well off as those located along the Grand Trunk Pacific fifty or seventy miles from Edmonton; but this is undoubtedly the case not only as regards those settlers located in the brush lands but those who have settled in the more open stretches. And one of the main reasons why I am opposed to the present immigration policy is that I do not think we have done our duty by the settlers who were induced to come into the country by promises of railway and other facilities. I do not suppose the government is prepared to spend a great deal of money for the construction of branch lines in western Canada. My constituency is not the only one that needs such accommodation, but we have been very anxious to get a railway built from Grande Prairie south to the Canadian National railway, thus giving us a short cut to the Pacific coast instead of hauling our produce two thousand miles and more to the east. However, unless we get relief of that kind I fear
we are going to lose the settlers who have * gone in there and tried to establish themselves during the past ten years. Therefore I cannot see the wisdom of drumming up settlers in the United States while we are losing the men who came in on the strength of these promises ten years ago.
Is it not a fact that about twenty thousand settlers have left that district?

No, not
yet. Ten thousand probably have left during the last four years but there was a population of 18,800 when the last census was taken. There are still about three million acres of settlement in that district, and the population, as I have said, is approximately about twenty thousand. The land is just as fertile as any in Canada. I repeat, the reason I am opposed to spending money to drum up settlers at the present t:me is because we can get the same results by retaining the settlers we have already if we are able to give them the railway facilities that they so urgently require.
Now, it may seem unreasonable to say that this government must fulfil all the promises and pledges given by immigration agents ten or fifteen years ago. I know it is difficult to pin down a corporation to redeem the promises made by an agent who may have acted more or less without instructions. Similarly it may be hard to pin down the government at the presept day to redeem all the promises made to these settlers in days gone by to induce them to come into the country; but the settlers are there, and if we are willing to spend a few million dollars to bring in more settlers, surely it is the part of wisdom to spend money to retain the settlers that we have already on the land. It will take the new settlers at least five years to become acquainted with the climatic conditions of the country and be as efficient farmers as those already settled there, while the latter have their equipment and are ready to go ahead under reasonably favourable conditions. I would make that constructive suggestion to the minister and government in the hope that he will be able to adopt it.
I hope also some means will be found to assist the returned soldiers located on these brush lands to clear their holdings. Most of them that I have seen during the past summer will pay about twice -as much to clear their farms as it will cost to buy new land under the method of clearing by hand.
I think in some instances mistakes were made. However, there is a way of clearing this land by fire, and I hope the department
