remove a great number of these unemployed
to the different dominions.
I am of opinion, Mr. Chairman, that only those immigrants desirous of living on the farm should be, at present, admitted to Canada, and what is more, be granted a little money to keep its people at home.
So as to relieve the industrial centres already too congested, the advantages of land settlement offered to foreign immigrants should also be offered to Canadians. I know, sir, that the government has already done a great deal in that way by settling the veterans on the land. In so doing they but wrote another page in the history of Canada; for the soldiers of the Carignan-Salieres regiment, those of the Scotch regiments who took part in the battle on the plains of Abraham, were the first in our country to drop the sword for the plough.
If it is good policy, sir, to encourage immigration on the farm, we must of all necessity encourage them to remain on Canadian soil. Statistics show to our regret, that most of the immigrants entering Canada between 1881 and 1922, have practically all left the country to emigrate to the United States. Sir Clifford Sifton refuses to blame the different governments that have succeeded one another, or put it down to the tariff, for the emigration of our people to the neighbouring republic. He acknowledges that with the exception of the French Canadians and a few others wishing to better themselves, those who left us were not worth much to Canada, and, they would have become, in a very short time, parasites.
The hon. Minister of the Interior intends to do a great deal to "repeople" Canada by encouraging a farming class of immigrants to this country who could buy farms on easy terms and by being given help from certain provinces so as to give to this campaign a more conclusive and practical object. The government gave proof of national spirit by organizing a special campaign encouraging the return to their native land of those French Canadians who left to establish themselves in the manufacturing centres of New England. If our friends on the opposite benches only wish to recall the fact, it was under the Conservative administration that the exodus of our people began. An hon. member belonging to the Progressive party, who is certainly not aware of the spirit of justice and equity which prevails in Quebec in regard to the distribution of government grants, asked the hon. Minister of the Interior, if the funds expended for the above-mentioned campaign would be applicable to the English speaking

Canadians. If so, there would be no grounds to be scandalized if we so insist on the repatriation of the French Canadians, because as pointed out recently by l'Ecole Sociale Populaire, in a communication to the Minister of the Interior, should not the province of Quebec which has been paying for the last twenty-five years for the recruiting of foreigners destined to other provinces, keep its people?
Canada has been up to now, if we are to put faith in statistics,-and statistics are occasionally reliable-a sieve for immigrants brought here at our expense. Henceforth, our immigrants should be possessed of a different spirit and their only desire before coming across to our country, should be to live here forever. I know, Sir, that we shall never be able to prevent all our immigrants from resisting the powerful attraction of the great country to the south of us; however, so as to diminish the attraction of that great magnet, let us make life easier for all the citizens of Canada by a wise and judicious administration. The government has decided to allow a certain class of immigrants to enter the country. Very well, but to keep them here we must first train them. The recruiting agent should certainly show practical results in the country where he is called upon to work, but we must give him an agriculturist, as an assistant who can advise the future settler on the character of the arable land, in the province where he intends to settle. Let not the immigrant come here and tempt fortune in a haphazard way.
What are to be the means employed to bring this campaign to a successful issue? An intelligent and truthful publicity carried on by agents speaking perfectly the language or the dialects of the country where they are sent to work.
Is the Civil Service Commission capable of selecting such agents? I refuse to believe it. The selection of such agents should be left to the minister, because qualified applicants may be easily found.
Mr. Chairman, shall this immigration be to the benefit only of the western provinces?
I do not think so. Let us consult the statistics of last year; the immigrants that settled in Ontario were more than 38 per cent, in the West 42 per cent and in the East about 18 per cent. While the other provinces were losing almost all their immigrants, Quebec, during the last twenty years, has kept the 500,000 immigrants it received plus 146,000 the natural increase of its population.
The government's project, as recommended by the hon. minister is very acceptable, since

Supply-Immigration
he provides in the majority of cases for the reimbursement of the money which he will have paid out to draw settlers to this country. The collateral securities that the immigrant will have to put up in certain instances will shelter the government against any loss. Let the government watch over the selection of those who are to settle here. The worthy immigrant may become intolerable and the latter may change and become undesirable.
Let the repatriation of our people take precedence over all the other means to "repeople" Canada. Let a thorough examination, both in regard to moral and physical fitness of the future citizens of Canada, be made at the embarkation port, and let us be especially assured that the applicant possesses the spirit which will allow him to accept the ways and customs of our country. Let us not commit that great blunder that befell a governor of a large French colony, who wanted "his black subjects to accept progress against their will." Our new settlers should be before and above all assimilable and we should not be obliged to alter entirely their notions in order to have them co-operate with us.
The primary requirements to be heeded, sir, are those in connection with human activities: when to act, how to act and in what limits to act?
A wise and prudent answer to each of these questions, will contain the whole policy of our government on the subject of immigration.
A scrupulous attention given to the selection of the new seeds which it is the intention to sow on Canadian soil* will produce presently a new wheat whose maturing ears, under this same sun of liberty and tolerance, will ripen into a truly Canadian nation. Such united efforts witout favouring sectionalism as regards the interests of the different provinces of confederation, will promote the progress of our beautiful Canada and enable it to fulfil the sublime destinies that Providence has reserved for it on this continent of America. That, sir, will be the eager aim and desirable outcome of a sound policy of immigration.

Mr. Chairman, I
have listened with a great deal of interest to the debate on immigration which has now been going on for some time. Some one made the statement to-day that possibly ninety per cent of the members who sit in this House were born on the farm; it would be interesting to know whether that estimate is true. If it is, I can only conclude, after listening to what a great many of the members have had to say, that some of them at least have very short memories; they have forgotten what living on a farm means. I thought 76J
from the speech of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) that he did not understand farming until he said that a person with a sound brain, much courage, and two pairs of capable hands could make a living when he turned his attention to cultivating the soil. I concluded then that the hon. member did understand farming. I was glad that the hon. member representing another Montreal constituency (Mr. Jacobs) spoke today because he made life on the farm and the difficulties which just now attend it so very plain that he saved me the trouble of doing so.
I believe that the real difficulty in Canada to-day is that there is too much difference between the standards of living of urban and rural people, and I believe that if we could re-adjust the rewards of life and effort we could solve the whole problem. Because the way to deal with the immigration problem is not to bring in new settlers, but to spread the present population more evenly over the country, in that way relieving congestion in the cities and avoiding the scarcity of population in the rural districts. I think that one of the things that makes people fight shy of working with their hands in this age is that as a nation we do not sufficiently respect those who toil with their hands. We have almost forgotten the biblical injunction that we were to earn our living by the sweat of our brow. I am amazed-and I feel that I would not be fair to myself, to my people or to the members of this House if I did not say so- I am truly amazed at the sentiments that are expressed by some of our well-groomed luxuriously living friends. They evidently have not had their brow wet with sweat for some time, or if they have their hands were not soiled with work on that occasion. I want to say right here that I respect more a person who knows what a good honest day's work is, a person who works with hand as well as brain, and -who works so hard that he or she goes to sleep aching with weariness, than I do those people who disdain the very idea of toil and try to make it appear to the world that they do not understand what actual work means.
So say we all.

I think that that is
at the very basis of this problem in Canada.
In connection with this immigration scheme one hon. member recommended bringing in servant girls to Canada to work in homes, to do the work that the woman of the house would do if she did not have a servant. But that girl is not considered the social equal of
Supply-Immigration

those for whom she works. Why not? If her character and her brain are as good is she not the equal in every way of the woman of the house who hires a servant simply because her husband is in a financial position to enable her to do so? I think it is time we were trying to even up social standards and not make such a difference between those who work with their hands and those who work with their heads-work exclusively with their heads, I mean.
I do not see why there should be such a great anxiety to bring into Canada more farmers and more farm labourers at this particular time. The farmers are already, with the help of the experimental farms and the 9 p.m. many things that have taught them how to produce abundantly, producing more than they can get rid of. There is no shortage of production, and yet it is sought to bring in more people into Canada to further produce when we are unable to consume what is already grown. This must have the effect of throwing upon the , markets of the world a surplus which must be consumed somewhere.
I am very much opposed at this time to any large expenditure of money for immigration purposes. I believe that the immigration offices which have been kept open for years should remain so, and that immigrants,-fit in body and mind-that offer to come here should be accepted; but that any great scheme of what I might call artificial immigration should be launched at this time is, I think, a mistake. A great deal has been said here about farming conditions in western Canada, but very little has been said about fanning conditions in Ontario. Consequently one would judge that people on the farms in that province were having a very pleasant time. That is not true. Farming in Ontario is right now passing through very strenuous times, and suffering more than it has done for a great many years. I received a letter, not more than a week ago, from the director of our organization in the township of Proton, Grey county, and in it he said that farming in Proton this year would not return them 3 per cent on the money invested. He also stated:
AH that is keeping us on the land is the fact that we cannot get off.
This letter did not come from a fanatic but from a man who is a successful farmer, as successful as farmers can be under existing conditions. I have heard it said many times that we have passed through the worst of the economic distress. I hope that is true, but I do not. believe that it is. If the revival of trade in Canada is to depend on the increased 
buying power of the agriculturist, I feel quite sure that that revival is yet some distance in the future. The unsettled condition of Europe has very much to do with poor prices for farm products. The depreciation of the currency in many European countries which prevents them from buying food which we so abundantly produce, and the high tariff against us which prevents our sending our foodstuffs into the United States, all make it look to me as though a revival of good times in Canada would be very slow in coming. If that be true, then why are we going to spend this year a vast sum of money, an increase of a good deal over a million dollars, to bring settlers to Canada to put on the land, to live under conditions which the people who have been on the land during good times cannot live through? If we want to help things in Canada, I would make this suggestion to the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) amongst the many dozens of other suggestions he has received. If he wants to cheapen living and to make life more livable in Canada, I would suggest that he import more manufacturers, doctors and lawyers and cheapen the cost to the producer, so that when we take sick we shall not have to spend so much in order to have a doctor come and see whether we are going to die or not, and when we scrap with our neighbour over something, the lawyer will not get the property of both.
That does not happen in Quebec. It may in Ontario.
I know we have some very gracious lawyers from Quebec. I am glad to learn that they would not do such a thing.
The same is true of the doctors. They would not see people die.

I really think this is not the scheme of the common people, neither the farmers nor the labourers, nor the ordinary working business people. I really believe this scheme has been carefully prepared by those most interested in immigration, by those who would reap the reward of the labour of the immigrant. They have always been interested in immigration and they will always continue to be. I think it is quite possible that railway and steamship magnates, financial knights, land corporations and the government which they control, have more to do with this scheme than the people. The United Farmers' convention, in December of last year-and I am proud to call myself a representative in the House of Commons of Ontario agriculture-passed this resolution:

Supply-Immigration
Resolved that this convention is utterly opposed to any system of state-aided immigration of agricultural workers or prospective land owners until economic conditions are so changed as to ensure the retention on the land of a fair proportion of those born there.
The whole question of immigration is one of economics. If you can make farming conditions in Ontario, in Quebec-because the farmers in Quebec are not very well represented in this House-in the Maritime provinces and in western Canada, livable, so that the people who work long hours, who have hands which bear the marks of much toil, who are faithful, who have courage, can, as a reward of their toil when applied to the land, have a fair amount of the good things of this life, whether those good things are in pleasure, in enough property to keep them in comfort in their old days, in culture or anything else-when that is true, that is all the immigration agency you will need; and until that is true, until farming in Canada is able to hold the best blood that is bom on the land, you can spend all the people's money you want to spend in bringing people out and putting them on the land, but the best that are there wijl leave until conditions are rectified.

I will leave to members from the prairies to discuss this question more immediately in relation to the farming industry there, because they are so much better qualified to do so. I will only say that I do not at all approve the suggested arrangement with this colonization company.
There are two minor matters to which I wish to allude briefly. The first is this, and so far as I know it has not been mentioned by any of the speakers. The Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) told us, in fact we know that there is in vogue to-day a system whereby the railway agents of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National become agents of immigration to the extent that they solicit applications from farmers for labourers, and then they gurantee immediately and speedily to supply that labour from Britain or Europe. I object to that because the government have gone to a good deal of expense to inaugurate a system of employment bureaus,-and they have shut down private employment bureaus-the idea being that wherever any scarcity of labour existed, application would perforce be made to the nearest government bureau and they would keep in touch with labour conditions throughout Canada. If there was a shortage of labour in one place and a surplus in another, they would be in a position to supply,-to feed the labour out-where needed. If a demand arises, as it so often does on the prairies, for labour which is of a mere seasonal character, they are generally able to supply it from the farms or towns of Ontario where that labour could return. But under this system, these railway agents act as immigration agents and the result will be confusion. Suppose the employment bureau has decided that a certain amount of labour of an agricultural character is required and they have provided for that. They suddenly find that these so-called railway immigration agents in the prairies have got orders for a certain number of farm labourers and they have rushed them in, in excess of those that have been provided for by the bureau. The system is not a good one, in any case; the people who solicit emigrants in the Old Country or Europe should not be those who have a direct pecuniary interest. Very' often these agents in the Old Country are paid so much a head, and experience has showm that this is not a desirable practice. This system of having railway agents act as immigration agents is calculated to promote confusion with government bureaus, and the labour organizations strongly protest against it.
The other thing I want to draw attention to is the fact to which the minister alluded yesterday when he said: "We have no immigration agent in Norway". If there are in the world any people who make suitable settlers, they are Norwegians. I hardly put them second to the inhabitants of the British Isles. The latter are superior because they are familiar with our language, but beyond that, Norwegians and Swedes are in many cases better fitted to be pioneer settlers in this country than men from the British Isles, because in Norway and Sweden conditions in the rural districts are very similar to the bush districts of Quebec, northern Manitoba and British Columbia. Therefore, those people take more quickly to conditions existing in Canada when they come here. They make sturdy industrious settlers of the finest type, and they are very readily assimilated; in fact, the second generation cannot be distinguished from our native-born. They are a distinct advantage to our nation because they improve our blood. It is a notorious fact that nations in the northern part of Europe, brought up in a hard climate and under severe conditions, are of a more virile type than the peoples of southern . Europe. We were told last year when this question was under discussion, that we had an agent at Bucharest and another at Warsaw. I would suggest that they be [DOT]taken away from Bucharest and Warsaw and put into Norway and Sweden, and we would

get a better class of settlers from those countries.

I have a clipping which I took out pf a local paper and which is headed:
Norwegian fishermen on their way to the Coast.
I may say that the Norwegian makes the very best class of fisherman, next shall I say to the Scot. It says here that:
Twenty Norwegian fishermen bound for Vancouver and Prince Rupert to engage in fishing at these points passed through here to-night.
Now, that is a forerunner of the fishing immigration that I anticipate, and I think I can justly anticipate it in consequence of the steps the government is taking in deference to the report of what is termed the Duff Fisheries Commission to reduce the number of Jap 'fishermen. It is claimed out there by the . cannery men that ruin stares them in the face if they cannot have the labour of the Japanese; and yet within a few weeks of the publication of this report we find Norwegian fishermen on their way to take the place of these Japanese. And there are many more who will follow.
Now, that is all the criticism I wish to offer on the so-called policy as some hon. gentlemen sneeringly designated it, of the Minister of Immigration. I will go further. I will say that I congratulate the minister- and I say it in no spirit of sarcasm at all- not altogether on the policy that he has brought down but on that portion of it which he has not given to us. I say that, I repeat, in no spirit of cheap sarcasm, because I believe he has done a better service to this country in omitting a good deal of the policy which it was reported he would bring down. We heard a great deal about a much heralded immigration policy that would be introduced by the minister, but we did not hear anything about it from the minister himself. We heard it from a carefully arranged system of propaganda which was used to educate the public and incidentally to educate the minister himself into the idea that we should have the bars
Utr. Neill.]
flung down entirely and a huge bold immigration policy put into force. First of all, those who were anxious to see such a policy put into effect ran to the minister and told him, "We must have this policy because it is needed in the interests of the country." Then, they ran to the public, through the medium of the newspapers and other sources, and told the public in bated breath, "Oh, the minister is going to bring down a grand, broad policy"; and they return to the minister and tell him that the public expects this policy and he must come through. But I give the minister credit for having withstood the influences that were brought to bear upon him. That the pressure was great we have only to listen to some of the speeches that have been made here to be convinced; and we leam as much from the press during the past six months.
There is no question that there was a skilfully arranged propaganda to force the minister into such a position that he would have to bring down practically an open-door policy. There are a number of people, perhaps I might call them unthinking people without implying any reflection on their intelligence, who have not thoroughly studied 'this question, and who have a vague idea that after the Liberals got into power in 1896 there ensued a wave of prosperity. The Liberals have preached that so often that no doubt a number of people believe it; and I think they almost believe it themselves. Associated with that fallacy also is an equally vague idea that the prosperity that prevailed at that time was correlative to the big immigration policy that was in operation in the years immediately subsequent to 1896. But we must bear in .mind what the conditions were at that time. It is absurd to say that because something was successful then it will necessarily be successful now, when conditions have changed. What were the conditions then? There was absolutely free land, and abundance of it, close to the railways, and the markets of the world were crying for wheat. There was at least one transcontinental railway being constructed and later on there was another which took up the surplus labour that was not disposed to go on the land and become farmers. But what are the conditions to-day? There is no free land now. Land has been quoted at $18 to $25 an acre, and while that might not be costly under some conditions, it is surely costly in comparison with land which was got for nothing and which my hon. friends to my left say they can make nothing out of to-day. Hon. gentlemen to my left declare that out of that land which was free originally, a living 'cannot be derived to-day.

Supply-Immigration
I am justified therefore in the assertion that land is costly now. Besides this, it is remote; because if it is eighteen miles from a railway, my hon. friends to my left state-and I have every confidence in their correctness in this regard-it is beyond the limit at which you can profitably haul wheat to the market. So that summing up, there is no free land to-day, what land there is available is costly, it is remote, there is no railway construction, and there is practically no market, or at any rate a restricted one for wheat. And I shudder to think what the conditions in the prairies would be to-day if we had to compete with the wheat that Used to go to the European market from the south of Russia. If that wheat were being unloaded on the market to-day the conditions in the prairies would be a good deal worse than they are.
An hon. member on the opposite side, the name of whose constituency I regret I have never ascertained, but whose charming personality will never be effaced from my recollection, spoke about the unseen hand, the hidden interest. He also mentioned something about an Ethiopian in the woodpile. Well, I too seem to be able to smell an Ethiopian in the woodpile; but it is a different woodpile, and a slightly differently coloured Ethiopian. I maintain that there is good reason for the assertion that the real insistent demand, what I might call the original demand, for this bold immigration policy of letting down all the bars comes from but two sources. It is true it is put forward by many other bodies now, no doubt many were innocently intrigued by the skilful propaganda that has been carried out. There are many men who firmly and honestly, I think, believe that we should have such an immigration policy and who had nothing to do with the origination of this propaganda. But I am firmly convinced that the real insistent demand for this flood of immigration-cheap labour is really the term- comes from but two sources with which I will briefly deal. The first one is the transportation companies, and that applies as well to our own railways and steamships. I have here a cutting from a paper of last October, which says that the transportation men, a number of high officials of the railways and steamship companies waited on the Hon. Charles Stewart, and presented to him a memorandum urging the adoption of "an aggressive immigration policy." The companies represented at the conference were the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian National Railways, the White Star Dominion Line, the Cunard Line, and Anchor-Donaldson Line, and no doubt they represented other interests allied to them.
Now just consider the way in which these people submit this demand of theirs to the minister. They do not come and say "We represent a transportation company or a steamship company and we want the job of bringing over immigrants." Not at all; they were not so crude. It is the naivete of the thing that amuses me. They come and tell the minister, "We, acting on the high principle that what we suggest is in the best interests of Canada, demand in the name of Canada this bold immigration policy." This is very much on a par, I think, with the action of a delegation that might come to this House as representing, say, the interests of the brick manufacturers. Suppose such a delegation should say to the government that they demanded, in the name of the good of Canada, that we should pass a law, by reason of the danger of wooden houses being easily destroyed by fire and because of their short duration, that all houses should henceforth be made of brick. Now, what would be the first idea that would suggest itself to one's mind? Why, one would say, "You are not a good witness; you are an interested party. You may be acting for the good of Canada, but we have a shrewd suspicion that your mind is more filled with bricks than with any high principles about the interests of Canada."
The parallel, I think, is complete. It would be better, we should say with the Scriptures, to let another man praise thee and not thine own mouth. If the transportation companies want to bring people over to this country it is their legitimate right to do whatever they can to secure for themselves that traffic. But when they presume, in the alleged interests of Canada, to dictate to the minister what policy he shall adopt, that is entirely another thing and they are going beyond the bounds of reason.
The other body which, I claim, is at the back of this demand for a bold immigration policy is the large corporation of employers in Canada. Their ideal of a proper industrial condition is that there should be always a large surplus of idle population, a sort of bank of idleness, a bank of reserve labour from which they can draw when they need labour and obtain it without much competition and which, when they have used it to meet an emergency, they can put back on the shelf for the general public to warehouse against the time when it may be needed again. They want such a bank of labour which they can draw upon at their convenience and foist off upon the public when they are done with it.
Now, that used to be a popular idea and the world saw nothing wrong with it, but times have changed and the world has learned

Will the hon. gentleman permit a question? Why is the immigrant from southeastern Europe undesirable?

For many reasons. In many
instances he is not an agriculturist; he runs ' to small businesses and to city life. The principal reason, however, is that he is born in a southern climate and has not the vitality and the virility of the men from the north of Europe. He does not assimilate; he remains in colonies of his kind. Where we find the Norwegian soon calling himself not Jonsen but Johnstone, and may be governor of the state or a candidate for the presidency, the other man remains in his own environment and is more or less a city dweller.
I was going to say that for the reasons I have enunciated I appreciate the moderation of the policy brought down by the Minister of Immigration. But I do think he has made a slight mistake in his dealing with the prairies; I think he has, in a measure, put the cart before the horse. The idea seems to be to bring in a lot more farmers and that farming on the prairies will then be prosperous.
Supply-Immigration

I suggest that the other method be adopted; make your farmers prosperous on the prairies, and the immigrants will come of their own accord. It may be urged that that is a trite saying: "Yes, make them prosperous, but how?" My friends to the left, the Progressives, say, by a free trade policy. I think, Mr. Chairman, they do not say it with quite the assurance or with quite the emphasis they did last year. I may be wrong in that, and if so I olfer my apologies, but I do not think they are quite so insistent upon a policy of free trade as a panacea for all their evils as they were a year ago. At any rate, if it were to be at all successful it would have to be complete free trade; anything less than that would be so trivial a reduction in their costs as to be immaterial. Very well; we will allow for the sake of argument that if we have absolute free trade we benefit the farmer, but at the expense of the eastern portions of Canada, of the manufacturers of the East. That is too big a price. I do not want to be a party to ruining the eastern provinces for the benefit of my prairie friends. On the other hand, it is equally unthinkable, equally fatal for us to allow the prairie provinces to be depopulated-because that is eventually what must take place if they do not get relief.

The hon. member is making a presumption that is not correct. I do not know that the group of which I have the honour to be a member has ever taken the stand on free trade that he presupposes ; neither is it on [DOT] record on any of our platforms or incorporated in any of our teachings that we support that principle. It is something that has been thrown at us; it is not something we have subscribed to in any particular.	[DOT]

I am very glad to hear my hon. friend's statement. I would answer it by referring to the pages of Hansard.
If, then, we cannot agree on free trade, what is the remedy? Unfortunately the obvious remedy is an impossible one-reciprocity with the United States. That is out of court for the present; we cannot achieve it however much we may desire it. But there is another remedy that I suggest, and it is even more iconoclastic than the one I enunciated before about the population. Let us meet the United States people on their own ground. If they say they are going to have high protection, then we must say that we are going in also for protection. But if we do that, we should go in for all-round protection applied not only to the manufacturer but also to the farmer of the prairies. The

question then arises, how can you protect the farmer when his goods are exported? The suggestion I make is that in view of the long railway haul, the only one in the world applying to the production of wheat and therefore handicapping the prairies to a very serious extent, we should adopt a system on a sliding scale of bonusing the wheat of the country and thus put the prairie farmer on the same level as the eastern manufacturer. I know my friends will hold up their hands in holy horror and say that that is an unsound economic principle. But I do not care anything about theories or principles of that description. I never studied economics, but I learned in a hard school that where there was a grievous evil, a practical remedy should be applied to it. I suggest this as a practical remedy. Germany a few years ago, speaking in terms of the life of a nation, was almost solely agricultural-more so even than Canada is to-day, but by the adoption of this system; by the payment of bonuses to her native or imported industries, she had a long chance to become the economic mistress of- the world. Had she not gone mad in 1914 she would by this time practically dominate the world in matters of trade. That is the system I suggest we should use to-day. It may be all wrong; it may be against economic principles -but suggest a better one if you can! Now, speaking for my own district-because I would not presume to state the views of other parts of Canada-I believe the "middle of the road" policy, as he called it, of moderate immigration suggested by the minister will meet with the approval of my constituents. I will go further-and here I speak only personally; I think it will conduce ultimately to the best interests of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the immigration question is to my mind the most important of all those which have been debated during the present
session.
The hon. Minister of the Interior has given us a masterly outline of the policy which he proposes to follow in this respect. I must offer him my sincere congratulations and at the same time promise him my entire support. Our country, although in its infancjq has before it a most brilliant future. It has known days of prosperity as well as days ol depression. At present, it has a population of over 8,000,000. Its territory is very extensive. The natural resources are abundant, in fact inexhaustible. The soil is very fertile and large areas only await vigorous hands to yield crops sufficient to feed the whole of Europe. Although our industries are somewhat

Supply-Immigration
at a standstill, owing to unstable trade conditions, they are gradually picking up as the market becomes firmer. Our labouring class reduced to unemployment through the shortage of work are experiencing a rather serious crisis; however we notice a change for the better in their conditions. Nevertheless, I think it would be a great mistake at present to believe and especially to state, even on the floor of the House that the labouring class are satisfied with their present conditions. I congratulate the government for closing the gates to all the labouring class of immigrants. Its duty at present, is to better the living conditions of the workman by supplying his family and himself with the means of existence; as long as the normal economic situation is not reestablished we must not open wide our doors but keep them well closed.
I consider, Mr. Chairman, that the first duty of a good government is to furnish to all citizens the means of existence, it would be an unnational and unpatriotic policy to bring in immigrants belonging to the labour class, when misery still reigns in many homes as a result of unemployment. What we want, at present, in this country, are settlers, real settlers, it matters little whether they be English, French, Belgian, Italian, Jew or Scotch, as long as they can be assimilated, are sound' of body and mind, are not bolshevists, anarchists, nor socialists, are thoughtful of the moral and religious conditions and obedient to the laws of our country.
For the last few years, Mr. Chairman, farming, if I am to believe the doleful stories of our hon. friends the Progressives, does not give the same returns as it did previous to the war. I am of the same opinion; however, although the Condition of the farmer is very precarious, I think there is some exaggeration. That the western farmer's plight is more serious than that of the eastern farmer, I am ready to acknowledge. The hon. Ministe" gave us the true solution when he said: If we wish colonization to progress in the west, we must avoid past mistakes and not sell to the new settler more land than he can cultivate. The hon. Minister considers that 160 acres of land constitute a large farm; it is, indeed, ample for a settler if he desires to farm it with good results. That there mav be other reasons than those I have just given, that contribute in making farming in the West a poor paying proposition, such for instance as the high price of labour, the high freight rates and lack of transportation facilities, I admit; but I think the keynote of success for a farmer is to make the most of every inch of ground at his disposal and that all his
efforts must be concentrated with that aim in view, bettering as much as possible his method of farming and adapting it to the conditions of his land so as to husband its power of production indefinitely.
I do not wish, Mr. Chairman, to detain any longer the attention of the hon. members of this House, however before closing my remarks I would ask the hon. Minister to use discretion in his choice of immigration agents. Each country has its particular ways and the agent must necessarily be familiar with these conditions. I doubt very much if an agent having only English at his command and unacquainted with the particular ways of the people would be a success in Belgium or in France. Every agent must be fitted for the position, if we wish that the money we are going to vote be profitable to the country.
In the past, Sir, the government made use of the agents of transportation companies. I think it was a great mistake, for these agents were more interested in increasing the number of passengers, so as to show large increases in their business, rather than bring into the country desirable settlers. What we are in need of are settlers capable of being assimilated, sound of body and mind, desirous of entering our country with a view to settling down and become part of the great Canadian family and contribute to its prosperity.

During this debate there have been innumerable views put forward regarding the subject of population and of immigration. The only common ground that I have observed in the debate is that there should be an increase in population, that it is of great importance and of value to the state. It has been put forward that increase in population may be secured by increase in the birth rate, decrease in the death rate, diminotion of the exodus and by immigration.
As regards the first point, an increased birth rate, I do not know that I can give the minister any very valuable suggestions on how it can be secured, but I would wish to make use of a phrase which has occurred several times during the debate, and that is to let nature take its course. As regards the diminution of the death rate, that is necessarily a slow process. To attain it is a process of gradual education throughout the country, and that is now going on. We all recognize the advance that public health is making in the country. I do not think it reasonable to expect the advance in public health and an improvement in the death rate to occur in more than a gradual way, and that is now going on in as satisfactory a way as we can reasonably expect. There-
Supply-Immigration

fore, the minister cannot look to that as any substantial basis upon which to increase the population.
Then we come to the checking of the exodus from this county. What can the government do in this particular? I do not think that I can suggest anything to the government to secure this beyond what they could do if they saw fit. It would be a declaration to the country of a fixed determination to carry out a protective tariff policy. Now, while this at the present time is somewhat in force, it is not frankly put before the country. It is not put forward by the government as an article of their faith. The difficulty arising from this is that the country lacks the stimulus to the expansion of trade and industry that it otherwise, I believe, would secure. That being the case, and I presume that it will not be the policy of the government to make any such declaration, it comes to this, that the minister and the country will have to fall back upon immigration. I grant you that in any case the policy of immigration must be a very large and important factor under all the circumstances. Whatever the tariff policy of the government may be and whatever the death rate may be, I believe we must still look to immigration as a very important part of any policy to increase the population of this country. That being granted I ask, what principle should we adopt in carrying out our policy of immigration. I believe the principle we should adopt is to bring these people into those districts where they are needed, where the industries and occupations are suffering from a shortage of men to carry them on. That should be the true principle underlying our immigration policy, and I think that is the principle the minister proposes to carry out. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) this afternoon advanced the view that we should bring in immigrants, doubtless artisans and mechanics, and place them in the cities. In this way the labour market in the cities would be supplied and the tendency to drift from the rural districts into the centres of population would be lessened. It does not seem to me, however, that that can be regarded in any way as sound advice to the government, first of all because artisans are not needed to the same extent that farmers are; but in any case the adoption of such a policy would produce a condition of unemployment-without the advantage of populating the country districts. I therefore think the true principle is to attract to our country men of a class of occupation that we lack in Canada.

As regards the volume of immigration at which we should aim, I am not one of those who believe in crowding the country too rapidly. There is no advantage in it; quality is always better than quantity. I think the minister would be well advised were he to admit immigrants in generous numbers but under regulation and always governed by the idea of quality, the purpose being to procure suitable men who will be of substantial value to Canada.
Having advanced this view I would now ask: How are the immigrants to be distributed throughout the Dominion? That is an important question and One that, in my judgment, has not been given the attention or received the consideration in past years to which it was entitled. What has happened? The large proportion of immigrants arriving in Canada has been directed to the West. That was quite natural because the field of settlement lay there. The free lands were there, the movement was along the line of least resistance, and therefore an enormous number of immigrants proceeded to the West. I do not say the West received too many immigrants; I do not think it did. I do say, however, that other portions of Canada have not received the attention which was their due. It was an advantage to the whole of Canada for a large number of immigrants to go to the West, but other portions of the country should also have received attention.
The minister has referred to the various ways in which he proposes to deal with the different portions of the Dominion. Now, the needs of the country vary very greatly; so do the previous occupations of the immigrants. Their aspirations are also widely different. It is well that they should go to different portions of the Dominion, as prompted by their own wishes and in harmony with the needs of Canada. This is a matter in which we are keenly interested. This phase of the question has not received that attention from past governments that it was fairly entitled to, and we hope that the minister will now be able to make good this past deficiency. I am afraid, however, from what I heard him say this afternoon that his policy will not meet this situation. I will give my reason for that opinion. The minister has outlined an elaborate programme for the West. What is proposed to be done with respect to the East? The minister has an official in the United States who is occupying his time in repatriating Canadians to the province of Quebec. As regards the Maritime provinces the minister states that he has an official in London who is familiar with the needs of New Brunswick, that is Mr. Bowder. Now, Mr. Bow-

der has been in the employ of the Dominion government in London since the first of November, having been taken on on a ninety days' certificate. He had previously been in the New Brunswick office in London for some considerable period and remained there until that office was closed. After having served the ninety day period, an exten-
10 p.m. sion of another ninety days was granted. It does not seem to me, under the circumstances, that any very great regard has been shown for an officer holding such a responsible position. I do think that an official capable of doing effective and reasonably valuable. work in connection with the province of New Brunswick should hold a position of a more definite and permanent character than Mr. Bowder has been given.

speechtext:
My hon. friend's statement is news to me; I had not heard that. Does my hon. friend say that the Civil Service Commission would not appoint a Britisher to the office?
Mr. MacLAREN; The circumstances are these: I happen to know Mr. Bowder; I have taken an interest in him for several years. I received a letter from him dated London, February 8, 1923, in which he states:
I have been employed, on instructions from the Minister of Immigration and Colonization in the Dominion Emigration office. London, as a temporary employee on a 90 days certificate, which was renewed for a similar period again on the 29th ult.-
And so on. He tells me that he has applied to be appointed an immigration agent and asks me to interest myself in the matter. When I received his letter, I wrote to the Civil Service Commission, and this is the reply from the secretary of the commission under date of February 22:
I have your letter of the 20th instant enclosing some correspondence from the above named-
W. R. Bowder,
-who is anxious to obtain employment in connection with Canadian emigration work in the Old Country. His
letter has special reference to vacancies now being filled by competition under the auspices of this commission in Great Britain. In this connection he mentions in his letter that he had been, promised advice in the event of a vacancy occurring but that he received no notification of the above-mentioned vacancy, but had his attention called to it through an advertisement in the Gazette.
In reply, I am instructed to say that Mr. Bowder's application is on file in this office and would not be overlooked in the event of an bpportunity offering to consider him, but in the particular case under consideration, namely, the present vacancies in Great Britain, the commissioners have decid'd that applicants resident in England cannot be admitted. This decision was reached on the advice of the Department of Justice in view of the large number of candidates apparently possessing the qualifications required and resident in Canada.
I may add that information to the above effect is being sent to Mr. Bowder.
Mr. Bowder, I believe, has lived both in England and in Canada, and his residence at present in London grew out of the fact that he was in the New Brunswick London office. Perhaps the minister will have an opportunity of further investigation upon that point; but I would submit that an official holding such a position and suitable, as I think Mr. Bowder is, should have the status, the influence and the permanency of a permanent immigration agent.
I was trying to describe what I thought was too scanty consideration of the Maritime provinces in connection with the immigration policy. There is another point. I instanced the fact of there being in the United States a Dominion official whose duty is to secure and repatriate Canadians to the province of Quebec. The minister has told us that there is an official from Halifax who is now at Boston and who has a similar function. Perhaps the minister can inform us if this official at Boston is co-operating with the New Brunswick government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I suggested to him when meeting him in Chicago, I think, in October last, that he should go back to both provinces and get full information as to the requirements in these provinces.

If there is co-operation
obtained especially with the local government, that may be of advantage; but I see this difficulty, that he is representing two provinces, or perhaps three, and if that be the case, I do not anticipate that we, in New Brunswick, will get very great results from that arrangement. At the present time, there are in New Brunswick hundreds of vacant farms. I would suggest to the minister that he consider whether there could not be in reference to New Brunswick a somewhat simi-

lar arrangement on a smaller scale to that which he now has in reference to Quebec, under which arrangement there will be an official whose duty it will be to secure the return of former New Brunswick residents to New Brunswick. One would certainly rather see them all go to Quebec than not come to Canada. One does not wish to take any limited view; but we want to take the view that there is something coming, and I should like to have heard the minister say that he had a little more definite policy for each province. There must, of course, be a general policy; but if the minister would say we hope to do something for Quebec, something for Prince Edward Island, something for Nova Scotia and something for New Brunswick, we would feel there was something tangible in his policy. At the present time I feel that New Brunswick will get very little out of the policy as we have heard it enunciated. I may be mistaken about the matter; I shall be very glad to confess my mistake if the minister's policy should prove to be different; but I believe if we can secure a more important appointment in the government's office in London, if we car have an official who will care especially for the repatriation of New Brunswickers from the United States and who will co-operate with the New Brunswick government, we shall make a substantial advance, something that is worth while.	v
As I said, there are in New Brunswick hundreds of vacant farms and while, naturally, it is easier for the Dominion government to concentrate more on the parts of the country where they have lands of their own, surely the duty of the government is to care for all the provinc.es. It is probably more difficult for the government to do that, but that is not sufficient reason why the needs of the provinces should be overlooked. I do not direct these remarks especially at the minister. He is only enunciating his policy, but what I have heard does not satisfy me that there is enough in it to make it a success for New Brunswick. What I am referring to more particularly is our past history, and: statistics will show that immigration to New Brunswick and, I presume to the other Maritime provinces due to the Dominion government's policy, has been extraordinarily small. I believe the minister can get more value for the money he spends in bringing men to take the vacant farms, than by putting the money into some of the other schemes he proposes to put it into. Perhaps the minister would be good enough to go further into this.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What my hon. friend is asking for has been promised

the New Brunswick government, that is, that Mr. Bowder would be operating in the Old Country, and that they would have a man who would work in their interest. They did not discuss the abandoned farms with me; but I wrote the particular agent who is operating in the United States in the interest of New Brunswick to keep closely in touch with the New Brunswick government and to try to fill the necessities as they arose of the province of New Brunswick. The same applies, of course, to Nova Scotia.

I think, with the minister, that is a vital matter. The local government will necessarily be familiar with the situation; its co-operation is essential, and there is no difficulty in obtaining the cooperation of any provincial government. There may be as regards expenditure of money, but that is a different matter.
The other point to which I wish to refer is this. I should like the minister, when he is replying to the many suggestions that have been made and the views that have been put forward, to tell us what arrangements are being made regarding the distribution of farm labourers and domestic servants. I understand that it is the policy to bring these two classes into the country in addition to farmers, and with that I am fully in accord. I think these are three classes of people who should receive the preference. Domestic servants and farm labourers are not the classes that would come from the United States. We cannot look to that country for them; we must go beyond the seas, and I hope especially to Great Britain. Are there any plans as regards the distribution of domestic servants throughout the country? Will these immigrants and the farm labourers be distributed throughout the Dominion?

I cannot wholly support the remarks which have been made expressing sympathy with the minister in regard to his policy, or rather his lack of policy. I cannot fall in line with the statements of my iconoclastic friend from British Columbia (Mr. Neill) who spoke a few moments ago except in so far as they deplore the attempt that has been made, and which has been wholly successful, to induce the minister and the government to adopt what will eventually become an absolutely open-door policy. If that is not the aim of the department why the appalling increase in the estimates this year?-why an increase of $1,316,400? In the past you can trace where in a decade hardly more money was spent than we propose to spend this year in the increase alone.

I shall have something to say in regard to that feature of the question in a moment. But I want to assure the minister of one thing, and that is that I am absolutely in favour of justifiable immigration. And when I say justifiable immigration I mean immigration that is purely voluntary and absolutely selected. In other words, it will be essential to maintain in European countries, whence immigrants can come, and in the United States, a staff of men inspecting medically and otherwise those who propose to come of their own volition.
The present policy-it seems that is the only word we can use to express ourselves in regard tcT the statement that has been presented by the minister-bears, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and others who sit behind the minister have said, the earmarks of pressure from some Ethiopian, or something of that kind. I entirely concur in that statement. Indeed, we cannot do otherwise than believe it. We find in a despatch printed in a western paper, forwarded from Ottawa, the statement that the inspection of intending immigrants before they depart from European ports to Canada is to be continued, and I want to congratulate the minister and his department on their firmness in this matter. But why should it be necessary for the minister to declare himself on behalf of Canada in this regard? It is because the transportation companies had asked that this system be dispensed with, according to the despatch. If this is true I want to brand it as one of the most appalling attempts that have ever been made in this or any other country to secure tonnage, for we can call it nothing else, for the steamship and transportation companies at the expense of the unfortunates who may be deported.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have no
brief for the steamship companies, but in fairness to them I should tell my hon. friend that there came from them no such request at all. There are a great many despatches that are issued from the capital and I may say that I knew nothing about this one. But the steamship companies would much prefer inspection on the other side of the water, and in fairness to them I think I should make that known.
Mr. GARf.AND (Bow River): I am glad to hear the minister say so. But if that is the case there has been a great change of heart on the part of these companies since his predecessor, Sir Clifford Sifton, held office. Speaking before the Toronto Board of Trade
not so long ago, Sir Clifford Sifton said that the shipping people were very hostile to attempts made to confine immigration to certain desirable people. The report says:
They did not care what kind of people-
I want you to note the words.
-were brought to Canada. All they wanted to do was to bring the people here.
I sincerely trust that that attitude on the part of the transportation companies has been overcome. I have listened with the greatest attention to the minister and have carefully noted the declarations of the government from the outset this session, and I have not heard a single word that would encourage me in the belief that the administration now in power in this country is about to launch any definite policy of amelioration or alleviation of conditions as they exist today in the agricultural districts. Undoubtedly, the programme of propaganda that was carried on during the summer must have inspired the hon. member for Comox-Alberni to the outburst he was guilty of a little while ago which I certainly enjoyed. But some of the propaganda is illuminating. We find that open-door immigration is urged upon the department in order to settle up vacant lands lying idle. And these are the reasons given:
For example, the settlement of one township of land now lying vacant and undeveloped would mean the construction of quite a group of new farm residences, barns, outbuildings, fences, etc., with a resultant demand for lumber, hardware, cement, and other building materials. It would mean an additional school or two. Farm machinery of all kinds would be re-auired. New roads and possibly bridges would have to be constructed calling for more road machinery, steel, cement, culverts and labor. The manufacture of these things would call for the profitable investment of capital, the employment of skilled workers in the work of manufacture, and of unskilled labor in the production of needed raw materials. In the haulage of raw materials to the factories, and food and clothing for the factory workers, and the finished products from factory to consumer, the railways would secure much needed traffic, and, as the township became producing, return traffic to the markets of the world.
We do not read one solitary word about what is to happen to the settler when he comes here; it is all filled with what is going to accrue to the great manufacturing and transportation interests. An hon. member (Mr. Marler) the other day rather intimated, perhaps unintentionally, as I am quite willing to believe, that we painted the picture of deplorable conditions in the West in too lurid a fashion. I assure him that, on the contrary, we do not paint it nearly as bad as it actually is. I have not yet heard a single member on this side of the House tell of the things which I could show the hon. gen-
Supply-Immigration

tleman, if he cared to witness them next summer, day after day in my own constituency. Let me try to give him an example.

Let me ask the hon.
gentleman a question. Are the western prairies worth while bringing immigrants to, or not?
Will the hon. member explain just what he means by that question?
Yes, I would like to know, is it possible for selected settlers to make a livelihood on the prairies providing they possess average intelligence?
Mr. Chairman, under present conditions on the prairies I say it is absolutely impossible-absolutely impossible.
Then it is absolutely no use to bring immigrants to the prairies at the present time?

Absolutely. That is what I shall endeavour to demonstrate before we get through. In my opinion there is no use spending millions lavishly to bring people to this country when those already here cannot make a living. An hon. member on the other side of the House said to me one day recently that the peasant from southeastern Europe who will dig himself into a hole or live in a sod shaek is the kind of man Canada wants. Well, even those poor devils are just as badly off as the rest. If you bring them in they will stay a little while and then leave us.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that everyone is insolvent in the three prairie provinces?

The actual condition is so close to it that we might as well call it so. In the province of Alberta out of 80,000 farmers 20,000 are absolutely insolvent, and the majority of the remainder are approaching that state rapidly. Thirteen million dollars will be required this year alone to renew farm mortgages in that province. In the southern portion that comes under the operation of the Drouth Area Relief Act no less than $25,000,000 of debt has been administered by the commissioner in charge of that act. That was the amount of indebtedness turned over to him to endeavour to apportion among the various creditors, but which has of course not been paid.

Will my hon. friend inform the committee who created these particular

mortgages and for what reason? Was it on account of over-buying or anything of that description? Possibly not.

Let me inform the hon. gentleman of this fact. Shortly after the war was over a policy of financial deflation was commenced and carried out with the most ruthless brutality by those who alone can carry out such a policy. The immediate result was deplorable. Let me give my hon. friend an example of my own. In the fall of 1920 I think it was-I speak from memory and am not quite certain that my dates are absolutely correct-had I been able to thresh and dispose of the crop I would have been able to pay all my debts. But I did not get it threshed that year until October, nor did my neighbours, and by that time the rapid toboggan of prices had commenced, and when we actually got our grain to the market not only were we unable to pay our debts out of the proceeds but we had to carry over heavy liabilities to the following year. Pressure was exerted by the banks-very gently at first, but very steadily, and we had to meet it. Subsequently our debts piled up and mortgages had to be taken out. Just to meet the mortgage interest and renewals alone that amount of money which I have mentioned was required. This is official information issued by the government of the province of Alberta.
Of course deflation has not been the only factor. Drouth has had something to do with the trouble, but this does not apply so greatly to the north. A particular instance I wish to cite is that of a very good friend of mine living in the district of Hanna ordinarily a fairly good district. He is interested in the work of parliament. I thought I would send him a copy of Hansard, and this is the letter I received from him in acknowledgement:
I received the first copy and my wife and I are very thankful to you for sending us Hansard this year. I assure you we appreciate it very much. In view of our financial condition we had discussed very seriously what item of our household expense we could dispense with or retrench in order to get Hansard as we wanted it very much.
Is it not lamentable that they had to squeeze and corner to find $3? That is not all. He also took the opportunity of telling me something about the conditions there. I know them fairly well but not in any detail. I may say that this man is one of those who works from daylight to dark, he never spares himself, and does not drink alcohol or smoke. He is a married man with a small family. He writes:
The financial position in this locality, as indeed I believe in all Alberta, is very serious. Farmers are unable to meet their taxes and consequently the schools
are closed.

Those are the facts, Mr. Chairman.
The banks have told us that not one cent will they advance until the indebtedness of the municipality to these institutions has been met. In Dowling lake municipality we have only three schools running at- the present time and in two of these schools the teachers are waiting for their salary until it becomes available. God only knows when that will be. Loan companies are compelling practically every farmer who is in arrears with his interest to become nothing but a tenant on land which we spent the best years of our life opening and developing, and now instead of owning the land we become tenants. I sold a 50-lb. hide last month for $1.80, 45 pounds of hide, 5 pounds dockage. The same day I bought a little pair of shoes for our little girl, the cheapest I could get, weight about 5 or 6 oz., price $3. Where is it all going to end?
That is the desperate condition these men are in. No one can appreciate who does not live among them the suffering, the misery, the depression, the despair they go through year after year. And the day has gone by-I think the House was warned of it last spring -when the hopeful effort of former years will be put into the preparation of the land for this season's crop. I had the honour of going around my constituency last summer speaking at meetings. Sometimes I had to take long drives at night time, and on three different occasions in the southern part of that country we met people driving towards the United States border by night. On one occasion a party was stuck in a sand hole with a Ford car piled to the top with blankets and bedding. These are the conditions. Does any hon. gentleman' think we can take an inexperienced immigrant from any part of Europe, put him out in that country without capital and expect him to make a success of farming? Do hon. members think that men with a capital of from SI,500 to $2,000 can go out there and make a success of it? They may remain a little while, but if present conditions exist- there is the root of the trouble-and if an attempt is not made to curb the exploitation of these people by the combines and by the transportation companies-which my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) spoke of as bleeding this country white, and I agree with him, if such enormous sums must be paid out in dividends to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific railway and other corporations every year, then I say there is little hope for the West. It would be far, far better not to bring settlers into that country.
Does my hon. friend suggest that the Canadian Pacific Railway shareholders should go without their dividends? I merely ask for information.

As long as the great mass of the people who are helping 77
build up this country are not getting any dividends whatever, although they are doing far harder work than the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I would say most emphatically, yes. I think we should endeavour to curb the profits of these corporations and allow the people who are working to build up the country to get some gain for their hard labour.
I cannot understand the attitude of some hon. gentlemen who talk of progressing from the farm to the city. Is it really progression? Should it be regarded as such? Why do we hear hon. members say that the ambition of the young, of those who want to get ahead, is to leave the farm and go to the cities? Why should it be so? Yet we find in the delightful pamphlets sent out by the Department of Immigration the most glowing prospects that await the immigrant who engages in agriculture. Listen to what we send to Europe. WTe say:
Come to this country. The call of the West is no vain call. It beckons the courageous, the thrifty, the industrious, from the Mother Country particularly, to a life that is essentially democratic and independent, to an industry that assures the most encouraging returns, the basic and the noblest industry in the world-agriculture.
And yet we are told that it is progression, that it is only the ambitious that leave agriculture and go to the cities. There are many more similar statements in these publications, and I think the minister would be well advised to go over them very carefully. I find the grossest misrepresentation in these statements. The poor man in a foreign country; the English or Scotch crofter, the Irish hill peasant, who read this sort of thing and saw that picture on the cover would think this was a land of milk and honey and golden grain; that there was nothing to it but to come here, get a quarter section, and become a millionaire. I suggest that the minister revise these descriptions. I could paint a different picture, and it would be more truthful than this is.
And less encouraging.
Exactly, and it would be my intention that it should be so, under present conditions.

Even at that, Mr. Chairman, the members of the British House of Commons are not altogether easy in their minds. In spite of the delightful literature that is sent over there, and the glowing language, I have no doubt, of those who speak on emigration in England, the members of the British House of Commons are doubtful as to the suitability and feasibility of this thing. Sir Mitchell Cotts, a National-Liberal, discussing this matter in the House of Commons, December 6th, 1922, suggested that a party of members of the House of Commons should visit the Dominion and watch the settlement of immigrants here. I wonder why they thought that was necessary? We know why it was necessary. Too many, as an article in the Journal not long afterward said, had fallen into the hands of land speculators who had exploited them to their own advantage. Too many had found it impossible to make a living out here. I have in my own district a number of Englishmen of a very fine type, from Yorkshire. They came there many years ago and homesteaded with myself. These men, every one of them, hate the day they came in here, and they are Britishers, not foreigners. Their wives regret their coming and are continually talking about the lovely place they had back home in Yorkshire. One of these men worked for the Earl of Ripon, and he is everlastingly talking of the glorious times he had on the Earl of Ripon's estate.
Is not that generally true of English people, even if you put them in a part of the country such as the Eastern Townships in Quebec, where things are not nearly as bad as in Alberta?
I have no doubt the hon. member asked that question for the purpose of making that statement. It may be quite true.
No, I asked for information.

Although I have lived for almost two years in Sherbrooke county, Quebec, I know nothing about the part the hon. member speaks of. The part I lived in is devoted almost entirely to mining. But the hon. member may be quite correct. I do know some splendid young English settlers in the West, and splendid English families, who are striving hard but are in a condition of desperation. I would be glad to take any hon. members of this House out with me this year and show them in my own constituency these things I am talking of. After all, Mr. Chairman, this thing of spending millions of dollars on immigration can be characterized as indirectly bonusing the transportation and steamship companies. That is what it amounts to. It is advertising in foreign countries and securing tonnage for them. The people of this country are not going to stand for it any longer.
Again, when we bring these people over here, we cannot keep them. I need not stress that point as almost every speaker who has preceded me in this debate has pointed out how rapidly immigrants are leaving this country. If further evidence is wanted I would refer hon. members to the fact that President Harding of the United States, supported by many members of congress, has been discussing: seriously the bringing in of an Immigration Registration Bill. The reason given is this: Growing out of complaints of the Commissioner General of Immigration of increased activity in the efforts to smuggle immigrants through from Canada, and from Mexico, into the United States over the international boundary, congress is showing a disposition not only to grant ample funds for the enforcement of the immigration laws, but there is also serious discussion of an alien registration law. We are, Mr. Chairman, simply being used as a back door for those who want to go to the States and do not wish to or cannot enter the country directly. I have no doubt that when the quota plan from foreign countries enforced by the United States is used up we will have a tremendous influx of settlers into Canada. There will be no question about it. They will come in but they will not stay here; they will, if they can possibly do so, cross the border into the United States. Representative L.
